abschnitte.text: In a **reservoir**, water is collected and stored. It flows down through pipes to a **power station** and drives **turbines** there, which produce electricity. One example is **Lake Sihl**: its water flows to the **Etzelwerk** in Altendorf, which produces railway power for the SBB. On the Aare below Bern, **Lake Wohlen** was created in 1920 for the Mühleberg power station. The **Klingnau Reservoir** in Aargau was created in 1935 and is today an important reserve for water birds.

A **pumped storage power station** works like a huge battery. When there is plenty of electricity, water is pumped up into an **upper lake**. When electricity is needed, the water flows down again and drives the turbines. A large example is **Nant de Drance** near Finhaut in the **Valais**. It lies between the reservoirs of Emosson and Vieux Emosson and was completed in 2022.

An **arch dam** is curved towards the lake. The pressure of the water is passed over the arch into the **valley sides**, so the wall can be thinner. The **Mauvoisin** dam in the Val de Bagnes is about 250 metres high and is among the highest arch dams in the world. Not every reservoir has a concrete wall: **Lake Mattmark** at the far end of the Saas valley is held back by a large **dam** of earth and rock.

The **Lago di Lei** lies mostly in Italy, but the dam stands on Swiss soil. For the construction, a small area around the wall was exchanged between Italy and Switzerland. Its water flows to power stations in the Grisons. At the **Emosson** reservoir, many **fossilised footprints** were found on a rock slab in 1976. They come from prehistoric reptiles and are about 250 million years old.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence dam in the Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world.
A large part of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower.

teile.einleitung: The yellow PostBuses travel everywhere in Switzerland, even to remote mountain villages and over high passes. Their horn with three notes is well known.
wichtigste: The PostBus horn sounds like “Tü-ta-to”.
Before tight bends the PostBus sounds its horn, so that others can hear it coming.
On a mountain postal road the PostBus has right of way.
The mountain postal road sign is blue with a yellow post horn.
Over most high passes, PostBuses run only in summer.
Before the PostBuses, stagecoaches ran over the passes.

abschnitte.text: In the past, horses pulled the **stagecoaches** over the passes. They brought travellers, letters and parcels to the villages. At the beginning of the 20th century the first **PostBuses** appeared. They gradually replaced the coaches. As well as people, they also carried **letters and parcels**.

The PostBus has a special **horn**. It plays three notes one after another that sound like “**Tü-ta-to**”. On pass roads the PostBus sounds its horn before **tight bends**. There you cannot see oncoming traffic. The horn warns the others that a large bus is coming.

Some mountain roads are marked as a **mountain postal road**. The sign is **blue** and shows a **yellow post horn**. On these roads the PostBus has **right of way**. Other vehicles must give way and follow the driver's instructions. In this way the large bus gets through safely even on narrow roads.

Most high **Alpine passes** are closed in winter because of snow. That is why the **pass PostBuses** run mainly in **summer**. Many walkers and tourists use them to get comfortably into the mountains. All year round, however, PostBuses also connect many villages that have no railway station.

gewusst: The yellow colour of the PostBuses is so well known in Switzerland that you recognise it immediately.
The melody of the post horn comes from the overture of the opera “William Tell” by Gioachino Rossini.

teile.einleitung: The Mississippi is the most important river of North America and flows right across the USA from north to south. Together with its tributary the Missouri, it forms one of the longest river systems in the world. Steamboats, cotton fields and the stories of Mark Twain have made it famous.
wichtigste: The Mississippi flows entirely within the USA.
It rises in Lake Itasca in the state of Minnesota.
After about 3,700 kilometres it flows into the Gulf of Mexico south of New Orleans.
Its largest tributaries are the Missouri and the Ohio.
The writer Mark Twain made the river famous with Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.
In the delta area lives the American alligator, which is no longer endangered today.

abschnitte.text: The Mississippi begins as a small stream at **Lake Itasca** in the north of the USA. From there it flows south past cities such as Minneapolis, St Louis and Memphis. At St Louis the long **Missouri** joins it, and later the water-rich Ohio is added. Shortly before the sea it forms a huge delta that looks like a bird's foot.

The catchment area of the Mississippi covers about 40 per cent of the area of the USA without Alaska. Water from over 30 states ends up in this river. The name comes from an Indigenous language and means roughly **great river**. In heavy rain there are enormous floods, for example in the great flood of 1927.

In the past many Indigenous peoples lived along the river and used it as a route for travel. In the 19th century big **paddle steamers** carried goods and people up and down. Cotton was grown in the fields in the south, often by enslaved people. Today long tows of barges carry grain, coal and oil on the Mississippi.

The writer **Mark Twain** grew up in Hannibal on the Mississippi and as a young man worked as a pilot on a steamboat. His pen name comes from the language of river boatmen and means two fathoms of water depth. In his books about **Tom Sawyer** and Huckleberry Finn, children have adventures on and beside the river. These stories are still read all over the world today.

In the swamps in the south lives the **American alligator**, which belongs to the family Alligatoridae. The genus Alligator has only two living species, the other being the Chinese alligator. It was scientifically described by François Marie Daudin, and the word alligator comes from the Spanish “el lagarto”, the lizard. On the Atlantic coast its natural range extends about as far as North Carolina.

Because alligators were heavily hunted, the USA classed them as an **endangered species** in 1967. Thanks to strict protection laws the population recovered, and in 1987 the authorities declared it fully recovered. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) today lists it as not threatened. It nevertheless remains formally listed and is in Appendix II of the species protection agreement **CITES**, because it looks similar to endangered crocodilian species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mouth area in which a river divides into many arms.
A river that flows into a larger river.
A steamship driven by large paddle wheels.
The whole area from which water flows into a river.
An international agreement that regulates trade in endangered animals and plants.

gewusst: River boatmen called out “mark twain” when the water was two fathoms, about 3.7 metres, deep.
A drop of water takes about three months to travel from Lake Itasca to the Gulf of Mexico.
American alligators can grow to over 4 metres long.

teile.einleitung: Thun is a town in the canton of Bern where the Aare flows out of Lake Thun. It is called the “gateway to the Bernese Oberland” and is known for its castle and its special old town.
wichtigste: Thun bears the nickname “gateway to the Bernese Oberland”.
In 2024 about 44,000 people lived in Thun.
The great tower of Thun Castle was built by the Dukes of Zähringen.
The tower has four small corner turrets.
In the old town, pavements run on top of the shops.
The Obere Schleuse is a covered wooden bridge with a sluice.
Thun is the largest military training area of the Swiss Army.

abschnitte.text: High above the old town stands **Thun Castle**. Its great tower was built by the Dukes of **Zähringen** around the year 1200. The **four small corner turrets** are easy to recognise. Today there is a museum in the castle. From the top you can see far over the town, the lake and the mountains.

In the old town of Thun there is something rare: on the Obere Hauptgasse the **pavements run on top of the shops**. So you stroll along on the roofs of the shops below. The Aare flows right through the town. Over it leads the **Obere Schleuse**, a **covered wooden bridge** with which the water level can be regulated.

On the lake shore, in a large park, lies **Schadau Castle**. In the same park stands the **Thun Panorama**. It is one of the oldest **circular paintings** in the world and shows the **town of Thun** as it looked over 200 years ago. You stand in the middle and see the picture all around you.

Thun lies where the **Aare** leaves **Lake Thun**. From here the **Bernese Oberland** begins with its mountains and lakes, which is why Thun is called the “gateway to the Bernese Oberland”. In 2024 about **44,000** people lived in the town. It is one of the largest towns in the canton of Bern.

Thun is also well known to the **Swiss Army**. Here lies the **largest military training area** in the country. A training area is a site where soldiers are trained. In Thun many members of the army learn, for example, to drive and maintain vehicles.

gewusst: The Thun Panorama was created by the painter Marquard Wocher.
In Thun the Aare flows through the town in two arms and forms an island.

teile.einleitung: Lake Zug lies in central Switzerland between Zug and the Rigi. It belongs to three cantons and is known for a special fish, the Zuger Rötel. The Lorze flows through the lake.
wichtigste: Lake Zug borders the cantons of Zug, Schwyz and Lucerne.
It is about 14 kilometres long.
The Lorze flows into the lake and leaves it at Cham.
The Rigi rises on the south shore.
Arth lies at the southern end, the town of Zug on the north-eastern shore.
About 30 species of fish live in the lake.
The Zuger Rötel is a well-known speciality.

abschnitte.text: Lake Zug is about **13.7 kilometres** long, so around 14 kilometres. The largest part belongs to the canton of **Zug**. The south belongs to the canton of **Schwyz** and a small piece to **Lucerne**. The town of **Zug** lies on the north-eastern shore. At the southern end lies **Arth** in the canton of Schwyz.

abschnitte.titel: The Rigi on the south shore
abschnitte.text: At the southern end of the lake the **Rigi** rises steeply. It is often called the “Queen of the Mountains”. You can see the mountain very well from the lake. On the other side of the Rigi lies Lake Lucerne. So Lake Zug lies between gentle hills in the north and mountains in the south.

The **Lorze** flows into the lake west of the town of Zug. Shortly afterwards it leaves it again, at **Cham**. After that it flows on towards the **Reuss**. That is why people say the Lorze flows through Lake Zug. Some of its water comes from Lake Ägeri.

**32 species of fish** live in Lake Zug. Important food fish are **whitefish**, **perch** and **pike**. Especially well known is the **Zuger Rötel**. It is a special kind of **Arctic char**. The Rötel is a popular food fish and a speciality of the region.

gewusst: The Zuger Rötel is a special form of Arctic char found in Lake Zug.
The Lorze flows into Lake Zug and shortly afterwards out again at Cham.

teile.einleitung: The Thur is a river in eastern Switzerland. It rises near the Säntis, flows through the Toggenburg and Thurgau and finally joins the Rhine.
wichtigste: The Thur rises near the Säntis.
It flows through the Toggenburg in the canton of St Gallen.
Its course leads through the cantons of St Gallen, Thurgau and Zurich.
It is about 135 kilometres long and flows into the Rhine.
The canton of Thurgau is named after it.
Because no lake catches its water, it swells quickly when it rains.

abschnitte.text: The **Thur** rises in the area of the **Säntis**, the highest mountain in eastern Switzerland. After that it flows through the **Toggenburg**, a long valley in the canton of **St Gallen**. In this valley lie places such as Wildhaus, Unterwasser and Wattwil. The Toggenburg is strongly shaped by the Thur.

The Thur flows through the cantons of **St Gallen**, **Thurgau** and **Zurich**. In the canton of St Gallen it comes near **Wil**. In Thurgau, **Weinfelden** lies on its bank. **Thurgau** even takes its name from this river. In the canton of Zurich the Thur flows into the **Rhine** after about **135 kilometres**.

Many large Swiss rivers flow through a lake, for example the Aare through Lake Thun. The Thur does not. Because **no lake** catches the water, it can swell very quickly in heavy **rain** or snowmelt. Then in a short time it carries far more water than usual. That is why it was embanked in the past.

For a long time the Thur was forced into a straight bed. Today in some places it is given more **room** again. This is called **renaturation**. In this way gravel banks, floodplains and habitats for fish, birds and plants are created. At the same time the wider riverbed protects better against **floods**.

gewusst: In a flood, the Thur can carry many times its normal amount of water.
The name Thurgau means roughly “region on the Thur”.

teile.einleitung: The Simplon Pass is an Alpine pass in the canton of the Valais. It links Switzerland with Italy. For centuries merchants, soldiers and travellers have journeyed over this route.
wichtigste: The Simplon Pass links Brig in the Valais with Domodossola in Italy.
The top of the pass lies at about 2,000 metres above sea level.
From 1801 to 1805 Napoleon had the first carriage road built.
On the top of the pass stands a large golden eagle.
Beneath the pass runs the Simplon Tunnel, opened in 1906.
In the 17th century Kaspar Stockalper traded over the Simplon.

abschnitte.text: The **Simplon Pass** leads from **Brig** in the Upper Valais to **Domodossola** in Italy. The road climbs from Brig up to the top of the pass at about **2,000 metres** above sea level. On the south side it goes down again through a wild gorge. The pass is an important link between Switzerland and Italy. The road is mostly open in winter too.

In the 17th century the rich Valais merchant **Kaspar Jodok von Stockalper** used the Simplon for his trade. He traded mainly in **salt** and had the routes over the pass improved. With his wealth he built the great **Stockalper Palace** in Brig. It has three striking towers and is a landmark of Brig today.

Around 1800 **Napoleon** wanted to get across the Alps with his cannons. So from 1801 to 1805 he had the first **carriage road** built over the Simplon. Before that there was only a pack track for people and mules. On the pass stands a large **hospice**, a shelter for travellers. It is run by the same canons as the hospice on the Great St Bernard.

On the top of the pass stands a large **golden eagle**. It recalls the soldiers who guarded the border in the Second World War. Deep beneath the pass runs the **Simplon Tunnel**. It links Brig with Iselle in Italy and was opened in 1906. Trains run through it without having to climb over the pass.

gewusst: When it opened, the Simplon Tunnel was the longest railway tunnel in the world.
The three towers of the Stockalper Palace bear the names Kaspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

teile.einleitung: Piz Bernina is the highest mountain in the Grisons and the only four thousander in the Eastern Alps. It rises above the Upper Engadine near Pontresina, very close to the border with Italy.
wichtigste: Piz Bernina stands in the canton of the Grisons in the south of the Engadine.
The national map gives a height of 4,048 metres.
It is the highest mountain in the Grisons and the only four thousander in the Eastern Alps.
A famous snow ridge leads to the summit over the Biancograt.
From the Bernina massif the Morteratsch Glacier flows down into the valley.
“Piz” is the Romansh word for peak.

abschnitte.text: According to the Swiss **national map**, Piz Bernina is **4,048 metres** high. This makes it the **highest mountain in the Grisons**. It is also the **only four thousander in the Eastern Alps**. All the other four thousanders of the Alps stand further west, for example in the Valais or the Bernese Oberland. It rises above the **Upper Engadine** near Pontresina.

The **national border** runs just under 200 metres south of the summit. The summit itself therefore lies in Switzerland. On the south side lies the Italian valley of **Valmalenco** with the villages of Chiesa and Lanzada. The whole mountain range is called the **Bernina massif**. Nearby, the Bernina Pass also leads from the Engadine into the Val Poschiavo.

From the north the **Biancograt** leads to the summit. This is a long, narrow ridge of snow and ice. Because it rises so white and steep into the sky, it is often called the **stairway to heaven**. For mountaineers it is a famous but demanding route. You need a lot of experience and good equipment.

From the Bernina massif the **Morteratsch Glacier** flows far down into the valley. It is one of the best-known glaciers in the Grisons. Because of global warming it has shrunk greatly in recent decades. Along a walking path, signs show where the ice used to lie.

In the Engadine many people speak **Romansh**. That is why many mountains there have names with **Piz**. The word means **point** or **peak**. Examples are Piz Bernina, Piz Palü or Piz Morteratsch. Romansh is one of the four national languages of Switzerland.

gewusst: Piz Bernina was first climbed in 1850 by Johann Coaz, while he was surveying the area for the national map.
The Rhaetian Railway runs the Bernina Express over the Bernina Pass very close to the massif.

teile.einleitung: The precision industry makes very accurate parts and devices, often so small that you can hardly see them. In Switzerland it has a long tradition that is closely tied to watchmaking.
wichtigste: The precision industry in the Jura Arc developed mainly out of the watch industry.
Moutier is regarded as the centre of décolletage, the making of small turned parts.
The sliding headstock automatic lathe is known worldwide as the “Swiss-type” lathe.
Medical technology makes, for example, dental implants and hearing aids.
The industry's association is called Swissmem.
Polymechanic is a typical apprenticeship occupation.

abschnitte.text: In the **Jura Arc** from Geneva to Schaffhausen, watches have been made for centuries. For this you need tiny, very accurate parts. Many firms today also use this knowledge for **medical technology**, **electronics** and **mechanical engineering**. In **Moutier** in the Bernese Jura, **décolletage** developed, the production of the smallest turned parts. Such parts are now also needed for cars and medicine.

For small watch parts, the **sliding headstock automatic lathe** was developed in Switzerland in the 19th century. In it the workpiece is pushed through a **guide bush**. This makes it possible to produce very accurate, long and thin parts. Worldwide this machine is known as the **“Swiss-type” lathe**. In Moutier such automatic lathes are still built today.

A growing branch is **medical technology**, also called **medtech**. Swiss firms make, for example, **dental implants**, **hearing aids** and parts for **pacemakers**. This requires precision engineering skill, research and strict quality standards. A small fault could have big consequences for a patient.

The **CSEM**, the Swiss Centre for Electronics and Microtechnology, was founded in **1984** in **Neuchâtel**. It brings research in microtechnology and electronics into industry. **EPFL** in Lausanne is also an important partner. It runs a large institute for microtechnology and has a site in Neuchâtel.

A typical apprenticeship occupation is **polymechanic**. They make precise parts on machine tools. The **dual vocational training** with a company and a vocational school is regarded as a success factor. Swiss firms do not compete on low prices but on **quality**, innovation and specialist products. This high **added value** allows high wages despite the strong franc. The association **Swissmem** represents the machine, electrical and metal industry.

gewusst: Because of its many watch firms, the Jura Arc is sometimes also called “Watch Valley”.
The MEM industry is among the largest industrial employers in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Amazon in South America is the river with the greatest volume of water on Earth. It flows from the Andes in Peru right across Brazil to the Atlantic Ocean. Around it grows the largest rainforest in the world, home to countless animals and plants.
wichtigste: The Amazon carries more water than any other river in the world.
It flows through the largest rainforest in the world, in South America.
The Nile is usually regarded as the longest river in the world, but the Amazon is of similar length.
It rises in the Andes in Peru and flows into the Atlantic.
In the Amazon live river dolphins, anacondas, electric eels and armoured catfish.
The Amazon rainforest is threatened by deforestation.

abschnitte.text: The **Amazon** rises high in the **Andes** in Peru. From there it flows east right across Brazil. At the city of Manaus it meets the dark Rio Negro, and the two rivers flow side by side for a long way without mixing. After about 6,400 kilometres it flows into the Atlantic Ocean.

No river in the world carries as much water as the Amazon. On average, over 200,000 cubic metres of water per second flow into the sea. That is more than the water of the next seven largest rivers put together. Its **catchment area** is about 170 times as large as Switzerland.

Around the Amazon grows the largest **tropical rainforest** in the world. It covers large parts of Brazil and several neighbouring countries. The forest stores a great deal of carbon and is therefore important for the climate of the whole Earth. Through **deforestation** for pastures, fields and roads, a lot of rainforest is lost every year.

In the Amazon lives the pink **Amazon river dolphin**, a dolphin that lives in fresh water. The green anaconda is especially common in the Amazon and the Orinoco. Electric eels live in murky, low-oxygen lowland waters and can produce electric shocks. There are also piranhas and many armoured catfish, which belong to the catfish group.

Many **indigenous peoples** live on the Amazon and its tributaries, for example the Waorani in Ecuador. They know the forest and its animals very well. In 2022, fieldwork was done with Waorani, which went into the description of the northern green anaconda. For many people the river is the most important road, because they travel by boat.

The Spaniard **Francisco de Orellana** travelled the river in 1541 and 1542 as the first European all the way to the mouth. He reported fighting women and so recalled the **Amazons** of Greek legends. That is how the river got its name. To this day, not a single bridge crosses the main stream of the Amazon.

begriffe.erklaerung: The whole area from which water drains into a river.
Dense forest in warm regions where it rains a great deal.
Original inhabitants who lived in an area long before the Europeans arrived.
A smaller river that flows into a larger one.

gewusst: Not a single bridge crosses the main stream of the Amazon.
The largetooth sawfish, actually a sea fish, has been recorded in the Amazon about 1,340 kilometres from the sea.
At high tide, the sea pushes a wave upriver into the Amazon, which is called the Pororoca.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is often called the “water tower of Europe”. In its Alps rise great rivers that flow through many countries to the sea. Glaciers, lakes and plenty of precipitation make the small country very rich in water.
wichtigste: The Rhine, Rhône, Inn and Ticino rise in the Swiss Alps.
The Gotthard massif is regarded as the centre of the water tower.
Glaciers store a lot of water as ice.
In Switzerland there are about 1,500 lakes.
At the Lunghin Pass, the water divides towards three seas.
Switzerland has about 6 per cent of Europe's freshwater reserves.
More than half of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower (as of 2024).

abschnitte.text: A water tower is really a store from which water is distributed. Switzerland is called this because many great rivers rise in the **Alps**. The **Rhine**, **Rhône**, **Inn** and **Ticino** begin here. Almost all the rivers flow across the border into the **neighbouring countries**. In this way many countries of Europe receive water from the Swiss mountains.

The **Gotthard massif** is regarded as the centre of the water tower. Around the Gotthard rise the **Rhine**, **Rhône**, **Reuss** and **Ticino**. They flow away in different directions. The Rhine reaches the North Sea, the Rhône the Mediterranean, and the Ticino, by way of the Po, the Adriatic.

A **watershed** is a line at which rainwater runs off in different directions. In the Alps there are many such lines. Especially well known is the **Lunghin Pass** in the Engadine. There three great river systems meet. Depending on the side, a raindrop ends up in the **North Sea**, the **Black Sea** or the **Adriatic**.

The **glaciers** are huge masses of ice and store a lot of water. In summer they melt and release water into the rivers. There are also about **1,500 lakes**, many of them small mountain lakes. Switzerland makes up only about 0.4 per cent of Europe's area but has about **6 per cent** of its freshwater reserves.

Switzerland uses its plentiful water especially often to make **electricity**. In **hydropower plants**, flowing water drives turbines. Reservoirs in the mountains store water for later. More than half of the electricity produced in Switzerland comes from hydropower (as of 2024).

gewusst: Depending on the side, a raindrop at the Lunghin Pass can end up in three different seas.
The Inn flows by way of the Danube all the way to the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The Alps are the great mountain range of Switzerland. They cover about 60 per cent of the country and are home to special animals and plants.
wichtigste: The Alps cover about 60 per cent of Switzerland.
The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze at 4,634 metres.
The Rhine and the Rhone rise in the Swiss Alps.
Ibex, chamois and golden eagles live in the Alps.
A pass is a way over the mountains from one valley into another.
The higher you climb, the colder it gets.

abschnitte.text: The **Alps** stretch right across Switzerland. They cover about **60 per cent** of the country. Many peaks are over 4,000 metres high. The highest mountain in Switzerland is the **Dufourspitze** in the Monte Rosa massif at 4,634 metres. The Matterhorn and the Jungfrau are also well known.

The **ibex** lives high up in the rocks, and the males have long, curved horns. The **chamois** is very nimble and leaps safely over steep rocks. Its short horns are bent at the tip like a **hook**. The **golden eagle** has sharp eyes and strong claws and hunts hares and **marmots**. Marmots warn one another with loud whistles when an eagle comes.

The **edelweiss** is a white flower with felty leaves. It grows on stony meadows high up in the mountains. The felt protects the plant from cold, wind and strong sun. The edelweiss is **protected** and must not be picked. Further up the plants become smaller and smaller, until only mosses and lichens grow.

A **pass** is the lowest point between two mountains. Roads lead over it from one valley into the next, for example over the Gotthard. Great rivers such as the **Rhine** and the **Rhone** rise in the Swiss Alps. Their sources lie in the area of the Gotthard. That is why Switzerland is also called the water tower of Europe.

The higher you climb, the **colder** it gets. With every 100 metres of height it becomes on average a good half a degree colder. That is why there is often snow on high mountains, even in summer. In an **avalanche**, a lot of snow breaks loose and slides quickly down the slope. Avalanches are very dangerous, which is why there are avalanche barriers and warnings.

gewusst: In winter, marmots sleep for several months in their burrow under the ground.
The ibex once died out in Switzerland and was reintroduced in the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: The Ganges is the most important river in India and one of the great rivers of Asia. It rises in the Himalayas and, together with the Brahmaputra, forms the largest river delta in the world. For Hindus it is a holy river, which they revere as the goddess Ganga.
wichtigste: The Ganges is the most important river in India.
It is about 2,500 kilometres long.
Its source lies at the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas.
Together with the Brahmaputra it forms a huge delta in Bangladesh and India.
In Hinduism the river is regarded as holy and is called Ganga.
Hundreds of millions of people live in the catchment area of the Ganges.
The river is heavily polluted, so there are large programmes to clean it.

abschnitte.text: The **Ganges** begins at the **Gangotri Glacier** in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, high up in the Himalayas. The glacier mouth from which the water streams is called Gaumukh, which means cow's mouth. The source river is first called the Bhagirathi and joins the Alaknanda at Devprayag. From there the river bears the name Ganga, in English the Ganges.

At the city of Haridwar the Ganges leaves the mountains and flows into the broad **Gangetic Plain**. It flows east past cities such as Kanpur, Prayagraj and Varanasi. At Prayagraj the great tributary **Yamuna** joins it, having flowed past Delhi and Agra beforehand. The Gangetic Plain is one of the most fertile and most densely populated regions on Earth.

In Bangladesh the Ganges, called the Padma there, meets the **Brahmaputra**. Together they form the largest **river delta** in the world, which flows into the Bay of Bengal. Part of the delta is the **Sundarbans**, the largest mangrove forest on Earth. Bengal tigers live there, which can even swim. A side arm of the Ganges, the Hooghly, flows through the city of Kolkata, home to millions.

For Hindus the Ganges is the goddess **Ganga**, and a bath in the river is said to cleanse the soul. In the city of **Varanasi**, wide flights of steps, the ghats, lead down to the water, where pilgrims pray and bathe. Every few years the **Kumbh Mela** takes place in places such as Prayagraj, one of the largest religious festivals in the world. Many millions of people gather there.

In the Ganges lives the **Ganges river dolphin**, a river dolphin with a long, narrow snout. It can see almost nothing and finds its prey by echolocation, that is, with clicking sounds and echoes. The gharial, a crocodile with a very narrow snout, is also found here. Both animals are seriously endangered because the river is polluted and built up with dams.

The Ganges supplies very many people with water for drinking, washing and for the fields. At the same time, sewage from cities and factories flows into the river. That is why it is among the most **polluted** rivers in the world. The Indian government has therefore started large programmes to build sewage treatment plants and make the river cleaner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mouth area in which a river divides into many arms, often triangular like the Greek letter delta.
Wide stone steps that lead down to the water on the bank of the Ganges.
Trees that grow in salty water on tropical coasts and stand on stilt roots.
Animals make sounds and find their way by the echo that comes back.

gewusst: In German the word “Ganges” can also simply mean “des Ganges”, that is, of a “Gang” (tunnel in the earth): the pink fairy armadillo presumably closes its “Gang” with a vertical plate at its rear end and so presses earth firm.
In 2009 the Ganges river dolphin was declared India's national aquatic animal.
In the Sundarbans in the Ganges delta live tigers that regularly swim back and forth between islands.

teile.einleitung: Cable cars bring people comfortably up mountains and over deep valleys. In Switzerland there are especially many of them. There are various kinds, all pulled or carried by a cable.
wichtigste: A funicular runs on rails on the ground and is pulled by a cable.
On an aerial cableway the cabins hang freely from the cable.
On a gondola lift, many small cabins constantly circle round.
On an aerial tramway, two large cabins travel back and forth.
The Stoosbahn in the canton of Schwyz has been the steepest funicular in the world since 2017.

abschnitte.text: A **funicular** runs on **rails** on the ground. A strong cable pulls the car up the mountain. Often two cars are fixed to the same cable: when one goes up, the other goes down. The **Stoosbahn** in the canton of Schwyz has been the steepest funicular in the world since 2017. It overcomes a gradient of up to 110 per cent, and its round cabins rotate so that the floor always stays level.

On an **aerial cableway**, the cabins hang freely from the cable high above the ground. A special form is the **aerial tramway**. In it two large cabins travel back and forth. While one cabin goes up, the other goes down. In the middle of the route they pass each other.

On a **gondola lift**, many small cabins travel one behind the other on a **continuously circulating cable**. The cable runs constantly in a circle, so you can get in almost at any time. In the station the cabins slow down so that you can get in and out comfortably. **Chairlifts** work in a similar way, where you sit on open chairs. Such lifts are very common in ski areas.

gewusst: The cabins of the Stoosbahn look like large tubes that rotate depending on the gradient.
In Switzerland there are hundreds of cable cars, many of them in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is world famous for its cheese. Almost every region has its own varieties, made from milk according to old recipes. Many of them are named after the place they come from.
wichtigste: Gruyère comes from the Gruyère region in the canton of Fribourg.
The holes in Emmental are formed by gas that bacteria produce.
Appenzeller is rubbed with a secret herbal brine during ripening.
With the girolle, fine rosettes are scraped from Tête de Moine.
The AOP mark protects the origin of a cheese from a particular region.
A “moitié-moitié” fondue is made half of Gruyère and half of Vacherin fribourgeois.

abschnitte.titel: From the milk vat to the wheel
abschnitte.text: Cheese is made from milk. The cheesemaker adds **rennet** and lactic acid bacteria to make the milk set. The solid mass is cut up, warmed and pressed into moulds. After that the cheese goes into a brine bath and ripens in the **cheese cellar**, often for many months. The longer it ripens, the harder and spicier it usually becomes.

abschnitte.titel: Hard cheeses with a long history
abschnitte.text: **Gruyère** is named after the little town of Gruyères in the Gruyère region and is a hard cheese with the AOP mark. **Emmental**, from the Emmental valley, is known for its large, round holes. They arise because certain bacteria produce the gas **carbon dioxide** during ripening, which collects in the cheese mass. The extra hard **Sbrinz** comes from central Switzerland. In the past, pack animal drivers took it with mules over passes such as the Grimsel to Italy.

**Appenzeller** is regularly treated with a herbal brine whose exact recipe is a closely guarded secret. **Tête de Moine** comes from Bellelay in the Bernese Jura. With the **girolle**, a rotating scraper, thin rosettes are made from it. **Vacherin Mont-d'Or** is a soft winter cheese from the Vallée de Joux in the Vaud Jura. A ring of spruce bark holds it together and gives it a resinous taste.

**AOP** stands for “Appellation d'Origine Protégée”, in English protected designation of origin. A cheese with this mark must be made in a fixed region and from milk of that region. This way nobody elsewhere can make a cheese and simply call it Gruyère. **Tilsiter** also has an interesting origin: at the end of the 19th century, cheesemakers brought the recipe from the town of Tilsit in former East Prussia to Thurgau.

Cheese is part of well known Swiss dishes such as **fondue** and **raclette**. With fondue, cheese is melted in a pot and pieces of bread are dipped in. The Fribourg fondue “moitié-moitié” means “half and half”, because it is made half of Gruyère and half of Vacherin fribourgeois. With raclette, cheese is melted and eaten with potatoes. Many families in Switzerland eat these dishes mainly in winter.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are hundreds of different kinds of cheese.
The rind of Vacherin Mont-d'Or comes from spruce trees of the region and gives the cheese its typical taste.
Sbrinz is one of the hardest cheeses in Switzerland and is often eaten grated.

teile.einleitung: Lake Sihl in the canton of Schwyz looks like a natural lake, but was made by people. By surface area it is the largest reservoir in Switzerland. Its water supplies electricity for the railway.
wichtigste: Lake Sihl is a reservoir.
At almost 11 km² it is the largest reservoir in Switzerland by area.
It lies near the monastery village of Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.
The river Sihl is dammed.
The valley was flooded in 1937.
The Etzelwerk uses the water to produce railway power for the SBB.

abschnitte.titel: A lake made by human hand
abschnitte.text: **Lake Sihl** came into being when a **dam** was built and the valley was filled with water. It is therefore a **reservoir**. The river **Sihl**, after which the lake is named, is dammed. After a few years of building, the valley was flooded in 1937. Farms and houses in the valley had to be given up.

With almost **11 square kilometres**, no other reservoir in Switzerland has such a large area. Even so, Lake Sihl is only about **23 metres** deep. It fills a flat **high valley**. The lake lies in the district of Einsiedeln in the canton of **Schwyz**. Very close by stands **Einsiedeln Abbey**, a famous place of pilgrimage.

The water of Lake Sihl drives the **Etzelwerk**. This power station supplies **railway power** for the SBB. It began working in the same year in which the valley was flooded. When the lake was built, two long bridges were put up across the lake, so called **viaducts**. Cars can cross Lake Sihl over them.

gewusst: In winter, Lake Sihl often freezes over.
Lake Sihl is popular with sailors, anglers and bathers.

teile.einleitung: Schaffhausen is a canton and a town right in the north of Switzerland. The canton lies largely north of the Rhine and is almost completely surrounded by Germany.
wichtigste: The town of Schaffhausen lies on the Rhine.
The canton borders Germany almost everywhere.
In the coat of arms a black ram leaps.
The landmark of the town is the Munot fortress.
The old town is known for its many oriel windows.
In the Klettgau a lot of wine is grown.

abschnitte.text: The canton of **Schaffhausen** lies largely **north of the Rhine**. It is almost completely surrounded by **Germany** and borders the cantons of Zurich and Thurgau only in the south. The town of Schaffhausen lies directly on the bank of the **Rhine**. In the past, ships had to unload their goods here, because further down the Rhine Falls blocked the way.
In the Schaffhausen **coat of arms**, a black **ram** leaps. It wears a golden crown. The animal suits the name of the town well. You can see the coat of arms on many buildings in the old town.

The landmark of the town is the **Munot**, a round fortress on a hill. It was built in the 16th century. In the tower hangs the **Munotglöggli** (Munot bell), which rings every evening at **9 pm**. In the past it signalled that the town gates were being closed. In the old moat, **fallow deer** have lived for a long time, and visitors can watch them from above.

The old town of Schaffhausen is known for its many **oriel windows**. An oriel is a small projecting part of a house wall with windows. In Schaffhausen there are over **170** of them, many artistically painted or decorated with figures. There are also splendidly painted **façades** to see, for example on the Haus zum Ritter.

In the **Klettgau**, for example in **Hallau**, many vines grow on sunny slopes. Especially well known is the red **Blauburgunder** (Pinot Noir). Right next to the town, in Neuhausen, lies the **Rhine Falls**, one of the most powerful waterfalls in Europe. It attracts many visitors every year.

gewusst: The Munot bell has rung every evening at 9 pm for centuries.
In the moat of an old fortress in the middle of the town, fallow deer live.

teile.einleitung: The Nile is one of the longest rivers on Earth and flows through north-eastern Africa to the Mediterranean. Without it, the advanced civilisation of the ancient Egyptians with their pyramids would never have existed. Even today, most people in Egypt live in a narrow green strip along the river.
wichtigste: The Nile is about 6,650 kilometres long and is regarded as one of the two longest rivers in the world.
It is formed from two source rivers, the White Nile and the Blue Nile.
The two arms join in Khartoum, the capital of Sudan.
The Nile flows into the Mediterranean in Egypt with a large delta.
In Egypt the pyramids stand near the Nile.
Since 1970 the Aswan Dam has held back the annual Nile flood.

abschnitte.text: The **White Nile** comes from the area of Lake Victoria in East Africa. The **Blue Nile** rises in Lake Tana in the highlands of Ethiopia. In Khartoum the two join and travel as one river north through the desert. Altogether the Nile touches about eleven countries of Africa.

In the past the Nile burst its banks every summer, because monsoon rain fell in the Ethiopian highlands. The water left fertile black **mud** on the fields. That is why the ancient Egyptians called their land “Kemet”, the black land. The Greek historian Herodotus therefore described Egypt as a gift of the Nile.

Over 5,000 years ago, one of the first great empires in the world arose on the Nile. The **pharaohs** had temples and the pyramids of Giza built near present-day Cairo. Stones and goods were transported by boat on the river. On the bank grew papyrus, from which the Egyptians made a kind of paper.

The **Aswan Dam** in southern Egypt was completed in 1970 and dams up the huge Lake Nasser. It protects against floods and supplies electricity and water for the fields. Since then, however, the fertile mud stays behind in the lake, and farmers have to use fertiliser. Ethiopia has also built an enormous dam on the Blue Nile, which led to a dispute with Egypt and Sudan.

In the Nile live Nile crocodiles, hippos and many species of fish such as the Nile perch. Countless migratory birds from Europe spend the winter in the swamps and in the **Nile Delta**. In South Sudan lies the Sudd, one of the largest swamp areas on Earth. For storks from Switzerland the Nile valley is an important route on the way to Africa.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of several rivers that together form a larger river.
A mouth area in which a river divides into many arms.
An artificial lake behind a dam wall.
A reed plant from which writing material was made in ancient Egypt.

gewusst: Whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer depends on exactly where you start measuring.
About 95 per cent of the people in Egypt live near the Nile.
When the Aswan Dam was built, the temples of Abu Simbel were sawn into blocks and rebuilt higher up.

teile.einleitung: Lake Brienz is a mountain lake in the Bernese Oberland and glows in a rich turquoise green. It lies between the village of Brienz and the town of Interlaken. Surrounded by steep mountains and waterfalls, it is one of the most beautiful lakes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Lake Brienz lies in the Bernese Oberland in the canton of Bern.
Its water is turquoise green because fine rock dust from glaciers floats in it.
The Aare flows first through Lake Brienz and then through Lake Thun.
Between Lake Brienz and Lake Thun lies the town of Interlaken.
The lake is about 14 kilometres long and about 260 metres deep at its deepest point.
Brienz is famous for its wood carving.
On the south shore the Giessbach Falls tumble down to the lake in several steps.

abschnitte.text: Lake Brienz lies at about 564 metres above sea level on the northern edge of the Bernese Alps. It is about 14 kilometres long, up to about 2.5 kilometres wide and has an area of about 30 square kilometres. At the eastern end lies the village of **Brienz**, at the western end the town of **Interlaken**. The lake is surprisingly deep: at its deepest point it measures about 260 metres.

The most important inflow is the **Aare**, which comes from the Haslital and flows into the lake at Brienz. At Bönigen the **Lütschine** flows in from the valleys of Grindelwald and Lauterbrunnen. At the western end the Aare leaves the lake again, flows through Interlaken and soon afterwards joins Lake Thun. In the past, Lake Brienz and Lake Thun probably formed a single large lake.

The glaciers in the mountains grind rock into very fine dust, which is called **glacial milk**. Streams and rivers carry this dust into the lake. The tiny particles float in the water and scatter the sunlight so that the lake glows turquoise green. The water is very clean and rather low in nutrients, so fewer fish live here than in some lakes of the Central Plateau.

Steep forests grow around the lake, and many streams plunge down the rock walls as waterfalls. Best known are the **Giessbach Falls**, which drop to the lake in 14 steps. Among the fish in the lake are whitefish, including the little **Brienzlig**, a kind of whitefish found only here. Lake trout also swim in the cool, clear water.

Brienz has been known for its **wood carving** since the 19th century, and there is a school of wood sculpture there. Above Brienz lies the **Ballenberg open-air museum**, where you can visit over a hundred old farmhouses from all over Switzerland. The little village of Iseltwald on the south shore is very popular with visitors from all over the world today. The people by the lake live mainly from tourism.

Passenger boats sail on the lake, including the historic **paddle steamer** “Lötschberg” from 1914. From Brienz the Brienz Rothorn Railway, a steam cog railway, runs up the Brienzer Rothorn. At the top you have a magnificent view of the turquoise lake and the Alps. An old funicular leads up to the Giessbach Falls and the Grand Hotel Giessbach.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water with very fine rock dust that comes from a glacier and looks milky.
A river or stream that flows into a lake.
A ship driven by a steam engine and large paddle wheels.
An outdoor museum where you can look at and enter real old houses.

gewusst: At about 260 metres, Lake Brienz is much deeper than neighbouring Lake Thun.
The Brienzlig is a small kind of whitefish that exists only in Lake Brienz.
The Brienz Rothorn Railway has run since 1892 and is still mostly operated with steam locomotives today.

teile.einleitung: The Uetliberg is Zurich's local mountain. It is about 870 metres high and offers a wide view over the city, Lake Zurich and as far as the Alps.
wichtigste: The Uetliberg is Zurich's local mountain.
It is about 870 metres high and belongs to the Albis chain.
The S10 train runs from the main station up to the Uetliberg.
The Uetliberg railway has been running since 1875.
It is regarded as the steepest standard-gauge railway without a cog rail in Europe.
There is a lookout tower on the summit.
The Planetary Trail leads to Felsenegg, and from there a cable car goes down to Adliswil.

abschnitte.text: The **Uetliberg** lies on the south-western edge of Zurich. It is about **870 metres** high and belongs to the chain of hills called the **Albis**. Because it is so close to the city, it is called Zurich's **local mountain**. On fine days you can look from the top over the city and Lake Zurich to the Alps.

From **Zurich main station**, the **S10** goes straight up the Uetliberg. The **Uetliberg railway** has existed since **1875**. It is regarded as the **steepest** standard-gauge railway without a cog rail in Europe. Standard gauge means that the rails are the same distance apart as on most SBB lines. Without a cog rail, the train stays on the track only through the friction on the rails.

On the summit there is a **lookout tower**. Anyone who climbs the many steps is rewarded with a panoramic view. Right next to it there is a restaurant. When there is fog over the Central Plateau, the Uetliberg sometimes sits above it in the sunshine, and you look out over a white sea of fog.

From the Uetliberg, a popular walking trail leads to **Felsenegg**. Along the way there are models of the **Sun** and the **planets**. That is why it is called the **Planetary Trail**. The distances between the models are reduced on the same scale as the planets themselves. From Felsenegg, a **cable car** goes down to **Adliswil**.

gewusst: On the Planetary Trail, the whole solar system is shrunk down to a few kilometres.
In winter the Uetliberg is often above the fog, while Zurich lies in the grey.

teile.einleitung: The Niesen is a striking mountain on Lake Thun in the Bernese Oberland. Because of its regular shape it is often called the “Swiss Pyramid”.
wichtigste: The Niesen stands on the south shore of Lake Thun in the canton of Bern.
It is about 2,362 metres high.
From a distance it looks like a pyramid.
A funicular railway runs up the Niesen.
Beside the railway a staircase with over 11,000 steps leads up.
Only once a year may people run up the staircase, in a race.

abschnitte.text: The Niesen rises on the **south shore of Lake Thun**. Its sides are evenly steep. That is why it looks like a **pyramid** from Thun or Spiez. It is about **2,362 metres** high. The mountain belongs to the **Bernese Oberland**, the mountain region south of Thun and around Interlaken.

The **Niesen Railway** is a **funicular**. Its cars are pulled up the steep slope on a strong cable. On the way you change into a second car in the middle. At the top, on the summit, you have a wide view over Lake Thun and of the mountains Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.

Beside the tracks of the Niesen Railway, a **staircase** leads up. It has over **11,000 steps** and is regarded as one of the longest staircases in the world. It was built for **railway staff**, so that workers can check the line. Normally it is closed to walkers.
Only **once a year** may runners use the staircase. In the **Niesen Run** they race step by step to the summit. It is very tiring, because the difference in height is almost 1,700 metres.

gewusst: The Niesen staircase is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the longest staircase in the world.
The Niesen lies between the Kander Valley and the Simmental.

teile.einleitung: Swiss watches are known all over the world. Watchmaking has a long history that began in Geneva and spread across the Jura. Today it is one of the most important export branches of Switzerland.
wichtigste: Calvin's ban on jewellery led goldsmiths in Geneva to take up watchmaking.
In the Jura, farming families made watch parts at home in winter.
The quartz watch triggered a severe crisis in the 1970s.
From 1983 the Swatch helped the industry to recover.
The COSC tests watch movements and awards the chronometer certificate.
Since 2020 the craft of watchmaking has been an intangible UNESCO cultural heritage of Switzerland and France.

abschnitte.text: In the 16th century the reformer **John Calvin** banned the wearing of jewellery in Geneva. Many goldsmiths lost their work as a result. They therefore turned to making **watches**, which were allowed as useful devices. In this way Geneva became an early centre of watchmaking. Later the craft spread into the **Jura Arc**.

In the harsh climate of the Jura, fieldwork rested during the long **winter**. Many farming families used this time to make watch parts in their parlours. From this arose the system of **établissage**. An entrepreneur, the établisseur, spread the making of the individual parts among many home workers. The parts were then assembled into the finished watch in one place.

In the 1970s cheap **quartz watches**, mainly from Japan and the USA, came onto the market. They pushed out many mechanical Swiss watches, and tens of thousands of jobs were lost in the Jura Arc. This period is called the **quartz crisis**. From 1983 the **Swatch**, a cheap plastic quartz watch with few components, helped the industry back onto its feet. It was made in large numbers and soon became very popular.

The official Swiss chronometer testing body **COSC** tests watch movements over several days in different positions and temperatures. Only especially accurate movements may call themselves **chronometers**. In the **Vallée de Joux**, with places such as Le Brassus and Le Sentier, watches with **complications** are made, for example moon phases or minute repeaters. The valley is regarded as the cradle of haute horlogerie, high watchmaking.

The Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, **FH** for short, has its seat in **Biel/Bienne**. Biel is also the headquarters of large watch groups. In 2020 Switzerland and France jointly had “watchmaking and art mechanics” inscribed as **intangible UNESCO cultural heritage**. That fits well, because the Jura Arc stretches across both countries. The watch towns of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle also belong to the UNESCO World Heritage.

gewusst: The streets of La Chaux-de-Fonds were planned in a chessboard pattern so that watchmakers had plenty of daylight in their workshops.
A minute repeater strikes the time with fine tones at the press of a button.

teile.einleitung: St Moritz lies in the Upper Engadine in the canton of the Grisons. The place is one of the best known holiday resorts in the world. Winter tourism in the Alps began here.
wichtigste: In 1864 the hotelier Johannes Badrutt founded winter tourism with a bet.
In 1878 the first electric light in Switzerland burned in the Hotel Kulm.
Even before that, St Moritz was known for its healing spring.
The Bernina line to Tirano has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.
The bobsleigh run to Celerina is built from natural ice every year.
At the White Turf, horses gallop over the frozen lake.

abschnitte.text: Long before winter tourism, St Moritz was well known. The iron rich **mineral spring** had been used centuries earlier. In summer guests came to the Engadine for a **cure**, to recover. In winter the hotels stood empty at that time. That changed with a famous bet.

In 1864 the hotelier **Johannes Badrutt** invited English summer guests to come in winter too. If they did not like it, he would pay for their journey. The guests came and stayed, delighted, until Easter. This is how **winter tourism** in the Alps began. In 1878 Badrutt had a small hydroelectric plant built in the **Hotel Kulm**, and there the first **electric light** in Switzerland burned.

The **Cresta Run** was built in 1884 by English guests. You ride down it on a heavy sled **on your front, head first**. The **Olympic bobsleigh run** from St Moritz to Celerina is rebuilt by hand from snow and water every winter. It is the only **natural ice track** for bobsleigh in the World Cup. St Moritz has already hosted the Alpine **World Ski Championships** several times, most recently in 2017 on its local mountain Corviglia.

At the **White Turf**, racehorses gallop over the frozen **Lake St Moritz**. These races have taken place in February for over 100 years. At the **Engadin Ski Marathon**, thousands of **cross country skiers** run from Maloja to S-chanf every March. The course is 42 kilometres long.

abschnitte.titel: By train into the World Heritage
abschnitte.text: The **Albula and Bernina lines** of the Rhaetian Railway have been **UNESCO World Heritage** since 2008. The Bernina line leads from St Moritz over the Bernina Pass to **Tirano** in Italy. In doing so it crosses the pass without any cog rail. On the way you see glaciers, lakes and many curves.

gewusst: In St Moritz the Winter Olympics took place in 1928 and 1948.

teile.einleitung: The Birs is a river in the Jura in north-western Switzerland. It flows through narrow rocky gorges called cluses and joins the Rhine in Basel. On its bank, the famous Battle of St Jakob an der Birs took place in 1444.
wichtigste: The Birs is about 73 kilometres long.
It rises near Tavannes in the Bernese Jura.
On its way it has cut through Jura folds and formed cluses.
It flows through the cantons of Bern, Jura, Basel-Landschaft, Solothurn and Basel-Stadt.
The Birs joins the Rhine in Basel.
In 1444 the Confederates fought the Armagnacs on the Birs.

abschnitte.text: The **Birs** rises near Tavannes in the Bernese Jura, very close to the rock gateway Pierre Pertuis. From there it flows via Moutier into the Delémont basin in the canton of Jura. After that it turns north and flows through the Laufental. Between Basel and Birsfelden it joins the Rhine.

The **Jura mountains** consist of many long folds of limestone. Over a very long time, the Birs has cut straight through several of these folds. Such breakthroughs are called **cluses**. A well-known one is the cluse near Moutier with steep rock walls.

On 26 August 1444, Confederate warriors fought the **Armagnacs** at **St Jakob an der Birs**. These were mercenaries led by the French crown prince. The Confederates were heavily outnumbered and almost all were killed. But because the Armagnacs themselves had suffered heavy losses, they withdrew afterwards.

Mills, sawmills and later factories used the power of the Birs early on. Villages and towns such as Laufen, Aesch and Münchenstein grew up along the river. Today a railway line and a road run through the valley. Near the Birs at Dornach, the **Battle of Dornach** also took place in 1499.

The Birs was long heavily built up and straightened. In recent decades some sections have been restored to a natural state, which is called **revitalisation**. Fish such as brown trout and grayling benefit from this. In Basel the banks of the Birs are a popular recreation area.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow gorge in which a river cuts straight through a mountain chain.
French mercenary troops in the 15th century.
A river that has been built over is made more natural again.
A long, wave-shaped mountain chain made of folded rock layers.

gewusst: In 1891, a railway bridge over the Birs collapsed at Münchenstein, one of the worst train accidents in Switzerland.
The municipality of Birsfelden near Basel is named after the river.

teile.einleitung: Dry meadows are lean, sunny meadows on dry soils. They are among the most species-rich habitats in Switzerland, but they have become rare and are therefore protected.
wichtigste: Since 1900, more than 95 per cent of Switzerland's dry meadows and dry pastures have been lost.
Since 2010 there has been a federal inventory of dry meadows and pastures of national importance.
A dry pasture is grazed, while a dry meadow is mown.
Dry meadows grow on shallow, permeable soils, often on south-facing slopes in the Alps.
Fertilising and scrub encroachment threaten them most.
Late mowing without fertiliser preserves them best.

abschnitte.text: A **dry meadow** is not fertilised. Unfertilised, species-rich meadows like this are generally called **lean meadows**, in contrast to fertilised **rich meadows**. Because there are few nutrients in the soil, no handful of strong plants grows up and smothers everything else. Instead, many different flowers, herbs and grasses thrive side by side.

Dry meadows are found where the soil dries out quickly. These are **shallow**, **permeable** soils, for example over limestone. In the Alps they are especially often on **south-facing slopes**, because the sun shines strongly there. Many semi-dry grasslands are shaped by the grass **upright brome**. It gave the plant community **Mesobromion** its name.

Whether it is a dry meadow or a **dry pasture** depends on how it is used. A dry meadow is **mown**, while a dry pasture is **grazed** by animals such as sheep, goats or cattle. Both need people: without use, bushes and trees would grow there over time.

Since **1900**, **more than 95 per cent** of dry meadows and pastures in Switzerland have disappeared. Many were **fertilised** so that more grass would grow, or built over. On remote slopes, by contrast, people stopped using the land, and the areas became **overgrown with scrub**. Fertilising and scrub encroachment are therefore the two greatest dangers.

In **2010**, the Federal Council brought into force the **Inventory of Dry Meadows and Pastures of National Importance**. It lists the most valuable areas. Farmers who look after such meadows receive support for it. The best approach is **late mowing without fertiliser**: this lets flowers bloom and scatter their seeds.

gewusst: Wild orchids often grow on dry meadows.
Many of Switzerland's butterflies and grasshoppers depend on dry meadows.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a country of winter sports. In the mountains many people ski or snowboard, and famous races draw spectators from all over the world. But climate change is setting ski resorts new challenges.
wichtigste: The Spengler Cup in ice hockey has been held in Davos since 1923.
The Lauberhorn race in Wengen has the longest downhill in the Ski World Cup.
At the Chuenisbärgli in Adelboden, a giant slalom is run every year.
The Alpine Ski World Championships 2027 take place in Crans-Montana.
Since 1992, the rotating gondola “Rotair” has run up the Titlis.
Laax is known for its big snow parks.
Saas-Fee is called the “Pearl of the Alps”.

abschnitte.text: Every year at the end of December, the **Spengler Cup** takes place in **Davos**. It is one of the oldest **ice hockey tournaments** in the world and has been held since **1923**. The host is HC Davos. Teams from different countries play there between Christmas and New Year.

In the **Bernese Oberland**, two big World Cup races take place every January. The **Lauberhorn race** in **Wengen** has the longest downhill in the Alpine Ski World Cup. In **Adelboden**, the best skiers race a giant slalom on the **Chuenisbärgli**, whose steep finish slope is famous. The **2027 Ski World Championships** take place in **Crans-Montana** in Valais. The resort already hosted a Ski World Championships in 1987.

In **Laax** in the Grisons there are big **snow parks** and a huge **halfpipe**. A halfpipe is a channel of snow in which you show jumps and tricks. International **snowboard** and **freeski** competitions take place in Laax. Freestyle means that it is about jumps and tricks, not speed.

Up the **Titlis** near **Engelberg**, the gondola **“Rotair”** has run since **1992**. It turns once around itself during the ride, so that all passengers see the whole panorama. **Saas-Fee** in Valais lies at about 1,800 metres and is surrounded by many four-thousanders. The resort is called the **“Pearl of the Alps”**, and no petrol cars drive in the village.

Because of **climate change**, there is often less snow at lower altitudes. Many ski resorts therefore use **snow cannons**. They spray water that freezes in cold air into **artificial snow**. But snow cannons need a lot of **water** and **electricity**. Some places therefore offer more activities without snow, such as hiking or tobogganing.

gewusst: The Lauberhorn downhill in Wengen is the longest course in the Alpine Ski World Cup.
St Moritz hosted the Winter Olympics twice, in 1928 and 1948.

teile.einleitung: Anyone travelling to Lake Maggiore or Lake Lugano sees many palm trees. They give Ticino a southern look. Most of them, however, do not come from here at all.
wichtigste: Many palm trees grow in Ticino, above all on the lakeshores.
This is possible because of the mild climate.
The most common palm is the windmill palm.
The windmill palm originally comes from China in Asia.
Its leaves look like a fan.
Today it is spreading in the woods and crowding out native plants.

abschnitte.text: In Ticino the **winters are mild**. The **Alps** keep out cold north winds, and the large **lakes** store warmth. It is mildest directly on the **lakeshores**. That is why especially many palm trees stand there, for example in **Lugano**, **Locarno** or Ascona. The area therefore feels almost like the Mediterranean.

The most common palm in Ticino is the **windmill palm**. It can also tolerate some **frost** and therefore grows well here. Its leaves are large and round and divided into many strips, like an open **fan**. The trunk is wrapped in brown **fibres**. In the past, ropes were made from such fibres, which is where the German name Hanfpalme (hemp palm) comes from.

The windmill palm originally comes from **China** in Asia. In the 19th century people began to plant it in gardens and parks in Ticino. Many villas on the lake were decorated in this exotic way. In time the palm became a symbol of Ticino.

Birds eat the fruits of the windmill palm and carry the seeds far away. In this way the palm spreads from the gardens into the **woods**. There young palms grow close together. They take light and space away from **native plants**. Experts call such plants **invasive neophytes**.

In Lake Maggiore lie the **Brissago Islands**. On the larger island there is a **botanical garden**. Plants from warm countries all over the world thrive there, for example from the Mediterranean region, Asia, America and Australia. You can reach the islands by boat.

gewusst: The windmill palm is among the most frost hardy palms in the world.
Neophytes are plants that humans have brought from other continents.

teile.einleitung: The Titlis is a glaciated mountain in central Switzerland above Engelberg. With cable cars, an ice cave and a suspension bridge, it is a popular destination for excursions.
wichtigste: The Titlis is about 3,238 metres high.
At the foot of the mountain lies the village of Engelberg.
The border between Obwalden and Bern runs over the summit.
It belongs to the Uri Alps in central Switzerland.
On the Titlis there is a glacier even in summer.
The “Rotair” gondola rotates during the ride.
The name probably goes back to the personal name Tutilo.

abschnitte.text: The **Titlis** is about **3,238 metres** high. It lies in **central Switzerland** and belongs to the mountain group of the **Uri Alps**. Over its summit runs the border between the cantons of **Obwalden** and **Bern**. At the top there is a **glacier** even in summer, so you can experience snow there all year round.

From the village of **Engelberg** at the foot of the mountain you go up with several lifts, past Lake Trübsee. The last stretch you cover with the **“Rotair”**. The special thing: the cabin **rotates** once completely around itself during the ride. This way every passenger sees the rocks, the glacier and the view all around.

On the Titlis you can go into a **glacier cave**. A passage leads right through the blue ice. Outside awaits the **“Titlis Cliff Walk”**. This is a narrow **suspension bridge** that runs along a rock wall high above the abyss. It is among the highest suspension bridges in Europe.

Where the name **Titlis** comes from is not entirely certain. It probably goes back to a personal name, namely **Tutilo**. A man of that name probably once owned land in the area. In the village of Engelberg a **monastery** has stood since the Middle Ages, still inhabited by monks today.

gewusst: When it opened, the “Rotair” was the first rotating aerial cableway cabin in the world.
Although the Titlis is developed from Engelberg in Obwalden, part of the summit lies in the canton of Bern.

teile.einleitung: The Thur is a river in eastern Switzerland that flows from the Säntis area to the Rhine. The canton of Thurgau is named after it. Because it flows through no lake, it is one of the wildest rivers on the Central Plateau.
wichtigste: The Thur is about 135 kilometres long.
It rises in the area of the Säntis and flows through the Toggenburg.
It flows through the cantons of St Gallen, Thurgau and Zurich.
The canton of Thurgau is named after the Thur.
Because it flows through no lake, it swells very quickly after rain.
It joins the Rhine at Flaach in the canton of Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The Thur begins in the uppermost **Toggenburg** at Wildhaus and Unterwasser at the foot of the Säntis and the Churfirsten. It flows north through Wattwil and turns east at Wil and then west. After that it crosses the broad Thur valley in the canton of Thurgau, past Weinfelden. At Flaach in the Zurich Weinland it joins the **Rhine**.

The Thur flows through no lake that could slow down or store its water. That is why after heavy rain or snowmelt it rises sharply within a few hours. In **times of high water** it can carry a hundred times more water than in a drought. In the 19th century it was therefore straightened and edged with dams.

Before the mouth lie the **Thur floodplains**, the largest floodplain landscape on the Swiss Central Plateau. For some years now the Thur has been allowed to flow freely there again and form new arms and gravel banks. This is called **renaturation**. Beavers, kingfishers, tree frogs and many rare plants live here.

**Thurgau** bears the name of the river that crosses it. Already in the Middle Ages the area was called Thurgau, that is, “Gau on the Thur”. The canton is known for fruit growing, especially apples, and is therefore also called Mostindien (“Cider India”). In the north it borders Lake Constance and the Rhine.

begriffe.erklaerung: Natural landscape beside a river that is flooded when the water is high.
When a river carries much more water than normal.
Making a straightened river more natural again.
An old word for a landscape or district.

gewusst: The Thur is one of the largest Swiss rivers whose water is not slowed down by a natural lake.
In the Thur floodplains, part of the region's drinking water is obtained from groundwater.
The Thur has two headwater streams, the Wildhauser Thur and the Säntisthur.

teile.einleitung: A cog railway can climb very steep mountains. Between the rails lies a rack, into which a cogwheel on the locomotive meshes. In Switzerland there are especially many such railways.
wichtigste: Cog railways have a rack between the rails.
Normal railways without a cogwheel are called adhesion railways.
The Rigi Railway of 1871 was the first mountain cog railway in Europe.
Eduard Locher invented the rack for the Pilatus Railway.
The Pilatus Railway is regarded as the steepest cog railway in the world.
A cog railway runs from Capolago up the Monte Generoso.
A cog railway runs from Montreux up the Rochers de Naye.

abschnitte.text: A normal train runs only thanks to the grip between wheel and rail. This is called **adhesion**, and such a railway is called an **adhesion railway**. On a steep gradient the wheels would spin. So a **cog railway** has a **rack** between the rails. A cogwheel on the locomotive meshes into it and pulls the train safely uphill and brakes it downhill.

The railway from **Vitznau** up the **Rigi** opened in **1871**. It was the **first mountain cog railway in Europe**. It was built to the system of **Niklaus Riggenbach**. His rack looks like a ladder, with the cogwheel meshing into the rungs. Many more mountain railways followed this example.

The **Pilatus Railway** near Lucerne has run from Alpnachstad up Pilatus since 1889. With a gradient of up to **48 per cent**, it is regarded as the steepest cog railway in the world. **Eduard Locher** invented a special rack for it. Two horizontal cogwheels mesh into it **from the side**. This way the cogwheel cannot jump out even on such a gradient.

In Ticino, the **Monte Generoso Railway** runs from **Capolago** on Lake Lugano to just below the summit. From the top you can see far over the **Po plain**. On Lake Geneva, a cog railway leads from **Montreux** via **Glion** up the **Rochers de Naye**. From there you look out over the whole of **Lake Geneva**. Railways such as the Gornergrat Railway and the Wengernalp Railway also run with a cogwheel.

gewusst: The Pilatus Railway overcomes gradients of up to 48 per cent.
Some railways run alternately with and without a cogwheel, depending on how steep the line is.

teile.einleitung: The Saane, called the Sarine in French, is a river in western Switzerland that flows from the Alps to the Aare. It flows through the bilingual city of Fribourg. Because it runs roughly where German and French meet, it has become a symbol of the language border.
wichtigste: The Saane is about 125 kilometres long.
It rises in the Alps at the Sanetsch Pass.
It flows through the cantons of Bern, Vaud and Fribourg.
In the city of Fribourg it has cut a deep gorge into the sandstone.
The Saane is often associated with the language border between German and French.
Below Bern it joins the Aare.

abschnitte.text: The Saane rises in the area of the **Sanetsch Pass** in the Western Alps. It flows through Gstaad and the Saanenland in the Bernese Oberland. After that it crosses the Vaud Pays-d'Enhaut with Château-d'Oex and the Gruyère region. After Fribourg and Lake Schiffenen, it joins the **Aare** at Wileroltigen.

abschnitte.titel: A river on the language border
abschnitte.text: In the canton of Fribourg, people west of the Saane mostly speak French and east of it often German. The real **language border**, however, does not follow the river exactly. Even so, people say jokingly that they live “ännet der Saane” (“beyond the Saane”) when they mean the other language region. The expression **Röstigraben** (“rösti ditch”) describes the differences between German-speaking Switzerland and French-speaking Switzerland.

The city of **Fribourg im Üechtland** was founded in 1157 by the Zähringen dukes on a rock above a loop of the Saane. It is bilingual, and street names are in German and French. The old town lies partly down by the river and partly up on the rock. High bridges such as the Poya Bridge span the deep Saane valley.

The Saane is dammed several times to generate electricity. The largest reservoir is **Lake Gruyère** in the canton of Fribourg, called Lac de la Gruyère in French. Lake Schiffenen below Fribourg is also a reservoir. For fish and plants these dams are an obstacle, so work is being done on better fish passages.

In the valley of the Saane lie well-known regions such as the Saanenland with Gstaad and the Gruyère region. The famous **Gruyère** cheese comes from the Gruyère region. The village of Saanen and the Saanenland bear the name of the river. Many walking trails and cycle routes run along the Saane.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line where one language region passes into another.
A joking word for the differences between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
An artificial lake behind a dam wall.
When two languages are officially spoken in a place.

gewusst: In Fribourg there is a dialect of its own called Bolz, which mixes German and French.
When the water level in Lake Gruyère is very low, old bridges and walls that sank in the reservoir sometimes appear.
The Saane and the Sense flow together very close to Laupen.

teile.einleitung: People with many different religions live in Switzerland, and many with no religion. The distribution has changed greatly in recent decades.
wichtigste: In 2022, people with no religious affiliation were the largest group for the first time, at about 34 per cent.
About 32 per cent belonged to the Roman Catholic Church in 2022.
In 1970 hardly anyone had no religious affiliation, only about 1 per cent.
About 6 per cent belonged to an Islamic faith community in 2022.
The relationship between church and state is regulated by the cantons.
Geneva and Neuchâtel have a far reaching separation of church and state.

abschnitte.text: For a long time two churches shaped Switzerland: the **Roman Catholic** and the **Evangelical Reformed**. The Reformation in the 16th century, for example in Zurich and Geneva, divided the country into Reformed and Catholic areas. For a long time the Reformed were in the majority. In the 20th century many workers came from **Italy, Spain and Portugal**, who were mostly Catholic. As a result the Catholics became larger in number.

According to figures from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO), in 1970 only about 1 per cent had **no religious affiliation**, and around 2000 about 11 per cent. In 2022 it was about 34 per cent. This put them for the first time ahead of the Roman Catholics at about 32 per cent and of the Reformed. The figures refer to the population aged 15 and over. There are big differences between the cantons: in **Appenzell Innerrhoden** in 2022 only about 15 per cent had no religious affiliation, and in Basel-Stadt and Neuchâtel more than half.

About 6 per cent belonged in 2022 to an **Islamic** faith community, many with roots in the Western Balkans or in Turkey. The share of other Christian communities, for example Orthodox churches, is the same size. In addition there are smaller groups such as Jews, Hindus and Buddhists. The Federal Constitution guarantees **freedom of belief and conscience**: everyone may freely choose their religion or have none.

How churches and the state work together is decided by the **cantons**. In many cantons the large churches are recognised as **cantonal churches** and can levy church taxes. **Geneva** separated church and state in 1907, **Neuchâtel** in 1941. There is no church tax in the usual sense there.

The Federal Constitution used to contain exceptional articles from the time of the **Kulturkampf** (culture struggle). The ban on the Jesuits was dropped in 1973. On 10 June 2001 the people and the cantons deleted the **diocese article**, which made new dioceses dependent on approval by the Confederation. On 29 November 2009 the electorate accepted the initiative against the building of **minarets** with about 57.5 per cent. Supporters and opponents had debated it long and fiercely.

gewusst: As late as 1970, almost the whole population was a member of one of the two large churches.
Since 2009 the Federal Constitution has banned the building of new minarets.

teile.einleitung: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest and oldest lake on Earth. It holds about a fifth of all the liquid fresh water in the world. Many of the animals that live here are found nowhere else.
wichtigste: Lake Baikal lies in the south of Siberia in Russia.
At about 1,640 metres it is the deepest lake on Earth.
It contains about a fifth of the world's liquid fresh water.
It is about 25 million years old and so the oldest lake in the world.
Over 300 rivers flow into it, but only the Angara flows out.
Since 1996 Lake Baikal has been a UNESCO World Heritage site.

abschnitte.text: Lake Baikal lies near the border with Mongolia, not far from the city of **Irkutsk**. It is about 640 kilometres long but only about 25 to 80 kilometres wide. Its area is about three quarters as large as the whole of Switzerland. Mountains rise all around, and the **Trans-Siberian Railway** runs along the south shore.

At its deepest point Lake Baikal is about 1,640 metres deep. It lies in a **rift valley**, where the Earth's crust is slowly pulling apart. That is why the lake grows a tiny bit wider every year. Because it is so deep, it holds more water than all the Great Lakes of North America put together.

The water of Lake Baikal is very clean and so clear that in some places you can see 40 metres down. In winter the lake freezes over for several months. The ice often becomes over a metre thick and is sometimes turquoise blue and transparent. Then people drive across the lake in cars and cut **ice holes** for fishing.

In Lake Baikal lives the **Baikal seal**, the only seal in the world that lives only in fresh water. A well-known food fish is the omul, a kind of whitefish.
