This area is called the **Dreiländereck** (three country corner). The canton of Basel-Stadt borders Germany and France.

Many cantons have a national border. The **Valais** borders Italy in the south, for example at the Matterhorn, and France in the west near Martigny and Monthey. The **Grisons** borders Italy and Austria, for example in the Lower Engadine and near Samnaun. The canton of **St Gallen** also borders Austria and Liechtenstein in the Rhine Valley.

**Liechtenstein** lies between Switzerland and Austria and is smaller than many cantons. The shared border is only about **41 kilometres** long. **Germany** is quite different: it has over 80 million inhabitants. France has almost 70 million, Italy almost 60 million. In Liechtenstein people also pay with the Swiss franc.

Germany, France, Italy and Austria are members of the **European Union (EU)**. Switzerland and Liechtenstein do not belong to it. Liechtenstein is, however, a member of the **European Economic Area (EEA)**. Switzerland has concluded many agreements with the EU, which are called the **Bilateral Agreements**.

gewusst: Every day many people from Germany, France and Italy travel to work in Switzerland. They are called cross-border commuters.
Switzerland has its longest border with Italy.

teile.einleitung: The Ticino is the most important river in southern Switzerland and gave the canton of Ticino its name. It flows from the Alps through the Leventina into Lake Maggiore and on to Italy. Its water ends up in the Adriatic by way of the Po.
wichtigste: The Ticino is about 250 kilometres long, around 90 kilometres of which lie in Switzerland.
It rises near the Nufenen Pass in the Gotthard area.
The canton of Ticino bears the name of the river Ticino.
It flows through the Leventina and past Bellinzona.
At Magadino it flows into Lake Maggiore.
By way of the Po its water reaches the Adriatic Sea.

abschnitte.text: The Ticino rises near the **Nufenen Pass** and flows through the Val Bedretto to Airolo. In the Gotthard area the Rhine, Rhône and Reuss also rise. After that it flows through the long **Leventina** past Faido and Biasca. After Bellinzona it crosses the Magadino plain and flows into Lake Maggiore.

At Sesto Calende the Ticino leaves Lake Maggiore again. It then forms the border between the Italian regions of Piedmont and Lombardy for a stretch. At **Pavia** it joins the Po. With it, the water finally reaches the **Adriatic Sea**.

The Leventina is a narrow, steep valley with gorges and waterfalls. The Gotthard railway and the A2 motorway run through it towards the south. In the past, muleteers with mules crossed the Gotthard here. Today several **hydropower plants** use the drop of the river to generate electricity.

At the mouth into Lake Maggiore lies the nature reserve **Bolle di Magadino**. There are reeds, floodplain forests and shallow shore zones. Many migratory birds rest here on the way over the Alps. It is one of the most important wetlands in the south of Switzerland.

The river gave the **canton of Ticino** its name; in Italian both are called Ticino. In the fertile Magadino plain, vegetables and maize grow thanks to the water. In the past the Ticino often burst its banks, so it was straightened in the 19th century. Today people try to make individual sections more natural again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A crossing over a mountain, where a road or path leads over.
In the past, a man who brought goods over the Alps with pack animals.
A wet landscape such as a swamp, moor or reed area.
The place where a river flows into another river, a lake or the sea.

gewusst: The Ticino is the only large Swiss river whose water flows into the Adriatic.
In the south of Italy, along the Ticino there is a large nature park, the Parco del Ticino.
At Bellinzona, three medieval castles watch over the valley of the Ticino; they are UNESCO World Heritage.

teile.einleitung: The Röstigraben is a jokey name for the border between German speaking Switzerland and the French speaking Romandie. It stands for differences in language, culture and voting behaviour.
wichtigste: Rösti is regarded as a typical German Swiss dish and gave the ditch its name.
In the Romandie people speak of the “rideau de rösti”.
In the EEA vote of 1992 the ditch showed up especially clearly.
Often the parts of the country differ on European and social policy.
Today the urban rural divide is often more important.
For the contrast with Ticino, people speak of the Polentagraben.

abschnitte.text: **Rösti** made from grated potatoes is regarded as typical of **German speaking Switzerland**. That is why it jokingly stands for the German speaking side. The **Röstigraben** is therefore not a real border but an image. In the Romandie people often speak of the **“rideau de rösti”**, that is, the rösti curtain, or of the “barrière de rösti”. For the contrast with Italian speaking Switzerland there is, by analogy, the **Polentagraben**.

The language border arose as early as the **early Middle Ages**. At that time the **Burgundians** settled in the west and the **Alemanni** in the east. The Burgundians took over the Romance language of the population, while the Alemanni spoke Germanic. In this way the border between French and German gradually formed. A common image for this border is the river **Saane**.

abschnitte.titel: A deep divide in the First World War
abschnitte.text: In the **First World War** there was a deep divide between the parts of the country. Many German speaking Swiss leaned towards **Germany**, many Romands towards **France**. The writer **Carl Spitteler** warned of this split in 1914 in his speech “Our Swiss Standpoint”. He called on people to stick together and stay neutral.

The Röstigraben showed up especially clearly in the vote on **joining the EEA** on 6 December 1992. The Romandie clearly voted yes, German speaking Switzerland mostly voted no, and overall joining was narrowly rejected. Turnout was **78.7 per cent**, one of the highest figures since women's suffrage was introduced. Analyses show that the Romandie often votes more openly towards the **EU** and a strong **welfare state**. In recent years, however, the **urban rural divide** has often become more important: cities vote differently from rural municipalities.

Romands learn **Standard German** at school. In German speaking Switzerland, however, people mostly speak **Swiss German** in speech. This makes conversations harder and can increase the distance. Conversely, many German speaking Swiss find French hard. Often both sides therefore switch to English.

gewusst: The Röstigraben is not drawn on any map, but you often see it on maps of voting results.
The EEA vote of 1992 had one of the highest turnouts since women's suffrage was introduced in 1971.

teile.einleitung: A protection forest is a forest that shields people, houses, roads and railway lines from natural hazards. In Switzerland about half of the forest is protection forest.
wichtigste: Protection forest guards against avalanches, rockfall, landslides and floods.
About half of the Swiss forest is protection forest.
Clear felling is in principle forbidden in Swiss forests.
A mixed forest with young and old trees protects best.
Too much browsing by game endangers the young trees.
The Forest Police Act of 1876 was the first to protect the mountain forest.

abschnitte.text: In the mountains, trees hold the **soil** in place with their roots. Their trunks slow down rolling **stones**, and their crowns stop a lot of snow from breaking loose as an **avalanche**. In this way the **protection forest** shields villages, roads and railway lines. About **half** of the Swiss forest area protects people and property from natural hazards.

In the 19th century, large areas of forest were cut down on many mountain slopes. After that there were severe **floods**. People realised that bare slopes are dangerous. The **Forest Police Act** of **1876** therefore banned large scale clearing in the mountains. Even today, **clear felling** is in principle forbidden in Swiss forests, that is, cutting down a large area all at once.

A **mixed forest** with trees of every age protects best. Such a layered forest stays stable even when single trees die. In the high mountain forest the **larch** often grows. It is the only native conifer that sheds its needles in autumn. Felled trunks are often left lying **across the slope**. Together with tall tree stumps, they slow snow and stones until young trees have grown back.

**Deer, roe deer and chamois** like to eat the buds and shoots of young trees. This is called **browsing**. If it is too heavy, no young trees can grow. The forest then becomes overaged and protects less well over time. Foresters and hunters therefore work together so that forest and game stay in balance.

abschnitte.titel: Planning by the Confederation and cantons
abschnitte.text: With the **SilvaProtect-CH** project, the Confederation uses models to work out where forest protects people and property from natural hazards. The **cantons** use this groundwork to mark out their protection forests. For their care there is the guideline **NaiS**, which stands for sustainability and performance monitoring in the protection forest. It lays down what a forest should look like depending on the natural hazard.

gewusst: A healthy protection forest is often much cheaper than avalanche barriers made of steel and concrete.
The larch loses its needles every autumn and first turns a bright golden yellow.

teile.einleitung: We need salt for cooking, for animals and, in winter, for the roads. Switzerland produces its own salt, deep from the ground. The Swiss Saltworks are responsible for this.
wichtigste: Schweizer Salinen AG belongs to all the cantons and the Principality of Liechtenstein.
Salt is produced at Schweizerhalle, Riburg and Bex.
In 1836 Carl Christian Friedrich Glenck found rock salt near Muttenz.
The salt is dissolved with fresh water pumped in and pumped up as brine.
The cantons' monopoly on the salt trade is called the salt regale.
Since 1922, iodine has been added to table salt.

abschnitte.text: **Schweizer Salinen AG** has its seat in Pratteln in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. It belongs to all the Swiss cantons and the Principality of Liechtenstein. Each canton has the sole right to the salt trade in its territory, the **salt regale**. The cantons have transferred this right to the Swiss Saltworks. The company runs the sites **Schweizerhalle** near Pratteln, **Riburg** near Möhlin and **Bex** in the canton of Vaud, which has belonged to it since 2021.

abschnitte.titel: How the salt got into the ground
abschnitte.text: The salt deposits on the High Rhine arose in the geological period of the **Triassic**. At that time a shallow sea evaporated in a hot climate, and the salt was left behind. Today these salt layers lie at a depth of about 100 to 400 metres. In 1836 the German saltworks expert **Carl Christian Friedrich Glenck** struck rock salt near Muttenz after several drillings. In 1837 the Schweizerhalle saltworks was opened.

At Schweizerhalle and Riburg, salt is produced by **borehole solution mining**. Fresh water is pumped into the salt layer. The water dissolves the salt and comes back up as saturated **brine**. After that the brine is purified and evaporated until only salt remains. At **Bex**, salt has been produced since the 17th century, and part of the roughly 50 kilometres of tunnels is open as a show mine.

The saltworks can produce up to about **600,000 tonnes** of salt a year. How much they really produce depends strongly on how much **road salt** is needed in winter. After shortages in hard winters, large stores were built, for example the **Saldome 2**, opened in 2012, for over 100,000 tonnes of de-icing salt. Since 1922, **iodine** has been added to table salt. The soils of Switzerland are low in iodine, and in the past many people suffered from a **goitre**.

gewusst: The Saldome 2 has a span of 120 metres and counts as the largest timber dome in Europe.
Thanks to iodised table salt, goitre has become rare in Switzerland today.

teile.einleitung: Lake Zurich is a large lake in the north of Switzerland. It stretches from the city of Zurich to the Linth region and borders three cantons. On its shores lie many villages, vineyards and swimming spots.
wichtigste: Lake Zurich borders the cantons of Zurich, Schwyz and St Gallen.
At its deepest point it is about 136 metres deep.
The sunny shore is called the Gold Coast, the other one jokingly the Sniffle Coast.
Rapperswil is called the “City of Roses”.
The Seedamm links Rapperswil with Pfäffikon SZ.
On the island of Ufenau stand a church and a chapel.
In 1853/54, remains of pile dwellings were discovered near Obermeilen.

abschnitte.text: The largest part of **Lake Zurich** belongs to the canton of **Zurich**. Smaller parts belong to **Schwyz** and **St Gallen**. At Rapperswil, the **Seedamm** divides the lake into two parts. Since **1878**, trains and cars have run there to **Pfäffikon SZ**. To the east of it lies the **Upper Lake**, where the **Linth** flows into the lake. At its deepest point between Herrliberg and Oberrieden the lake is about **136 metres** deep.

The shore between **Zollikon** and **Meilen** gets a lot of sun and has expensive houses. That is why it is called the **Gold Coast**. The opposite, left shore gets less sun. It is therefore jokingly called the **Pfnüselküste** (“Sniffle Coast”), because “Pfnüsel” means a cold. The **car ferry** between **Horgen** and **Meilen** links the two shores in about ten minutes.

**Rapperswil** in the canton of St Gallen is called the **“City of Roses”**, because thousands of roses bloom in several gardens. A castle towers over the old town. Not far away lies the island of **Ufenau**. There stand the church of **St Peter and Paul** and the chapel of **St Martin**. The island belongs to **Einsiedeln Abbey**.

In the winter of **1853/54**, the water level was very low. Near **Obermeilen**, piles and old objects came to light. The researcher **Ferdinand Keller** interpreted them as the remains of **pile-dwelling villages**. This discovery made pile dwellings known all over Europe. Today, pile-dwelling sites around the Alps are UNESCO World Heritage.

gewusst: “Pfnüselküste” comes from the Swiss word “Pfnüsel” for a cold.
The island of Ufenau has belonged to Einsiedeln Abbey for many centuries.

teile.einleitung: Lake Walen is a long, narrow lake in eastern Switzerland. It lies between steep mountains and is one of the most beautiful lakes in Switzerland. Its water flows on through the Linth Canal into Lake Zurich.
wichtigste: Lake Walen lies in eastern Switzerland between Lake Zurich and the Sarganserland.
Most of it belongs to the canton of St Gallen, and its western end also to Glarus.
The lake is about 24 square kilometres in area and up to about 150 metres deep.
Above the north shore, the seven peaks of the Churfirsten rise steeply.
The village of Quinten on the north shore has no road and is car-free.
Walenstadt lies at the eastern end, Weesen at the western end.

abschnitte.text: Lake Walen lies in **eastern Switzerland** and is about 15 kilometres long but only about 2 kilometres wide. Its area is about **24 square kilometres**. At its deepest point it measures around 151 metres. Most of it belongs to the canton of **St Gallen**, and its western end also to the canton of **Glarus**. Because high mountains frame the lake, its shores are very steep.

Above the north shore stand the **Churfirsten**, a chain of seven peaks. Towards the lake their rock faces drop away almost vertically. From the other side, from the Toggenburg, the mountains look gentle by comparison. At **Betlis**, the **Seerenbach Falls** plunge down over the rocks. They are among the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.

On the steep north shore lies the little village of **Quinten**. It has no road link. You can reach it only by **boat** or on a long walk. Because it is sheltered and sunny there, even vines and figs grow. The area is therefore sometimes called the Riviera of eastern Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The Linth and the Linth Canal
abschnitte.text: The **Linth** comes from the Glarus region and flows into Lake Walen. At the western end the water leaves the lake again. The **Linth Canal** then carries it on to **Lake Zurich**. In the past the Linth often flooded the plain. With the Linth Correction in the 19th century, it was tamed.

Along the **south shore** run the A3 motorway and the railway from Zurich to Chur. Because the slopes are so steep, they pass through many **tunnels and galleries**. Galleries are tunnels that are open on one side. In summer, passenger boats link the places on the lake.

gewusst: The Seerenbach Falls at Betlis are among the highest waterfalls in Switzerland.
In Quinten, thanks to the mild climate, vines and figs grow even though the lake lies between high mountains.

trcu20c.t: Coats of arms of the Swiss cantons

teile.einleitung: Each of the 26 Swiss cantons has its own coat of arms. The pictures and colours often tell something about the history of the canton. The coat of arms of Geneva is especially rich in symbols.
wichtigste: Each canton has its own coat of arms with fixed colours and symbols.
The Geneva coat of arms shows half an eagle and a golden key on red.
Above the Geneva coat of arms there is often a sun with the letters IHS.
Geneva's motto is “Post tenebras lux”.
The Valais coat of arms is white and red and shows stars.
Before 1848, Neuchâtel had a flag with chevrons.

abschnitte.titel: What is a coat of arms?
abschnitte.text: A **coat of arms** is a picture on a shield that stands for a family, a town or a country. In Switzerland each **canton** has its own coat of arms. You can see them on flags, offices and number plates. The study of coats of arms is called **heraldry**. The symbols often recall old rulers, saints or towns.

The Geneva coat of arms is divided vertically. On the left is half an **eagle** on gold, on the right a **golden key** on red. The key recalls the bishops who once ruled Geneva. Above the shield there often hovers a **sun** with the letters **IHS**. They stand for the name of Jesus in Greek.

The Latin motto **“Post tenebras lux”** belongs to the Geneva coat of arms. It means “After darkness, light”. The saying became important at the time of the **Reformation**, when Geneva was a stronghold of the reformer Calvin. It still often stands above the coat of arms today.

The **Valais coat of arms** is split vertically: **white** on the left, **red** on the right. Scattered over it are **stars** in the opposite colour. The stars stand for the districts of the canton, which in Valais are called Zenden. The coat of arms is easy to recognise and hangs on many houses.

Neuchâtel belonged for a long time to the king of **Prussia** and became a republic only in 1848. The old flag shows three silver **chevrons** on a red stripe on gold. It comes from the former counts of Neuchâtel. After the **revolution of 1848**, the canton received a new flag in green, white and red with a small Swiss cross. Some municipalities and clubs still use the old flag today.

gewusst: The letters IHS in the Geneva sun stand for the name of Jesus in Greek.
From 1815 Neuchâtel was a Swiss canton and at the same time, until 1848, a principality of the king of Prussia.

teile.einleitung: Sion, in German Sitten, is the capital of the canton of the Valais. The town lies in the Rhone valley and is one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. It is known for its two castle hills.
wichtigste: Sion is the capital of the canton of the Valais.
The old town lies at about 500 metres above sea level in the Rhone valley.
Above the town rise the hills of Valère and Tourbillon.
In the Basilica of Valère stands one of the oldest playable organs in the world.
In 2018 the voters of the Valais rejected the Olympic bid “Sion 2026”.

abschnitte.text: **Sion** is called **Sitten** in German and is the capital of the canton of the **Valais**. In the town people speak mainly French. The old town lies in the **Rhone valley** at about 500 metres above sea level. The mountains all around, however, are over 3,000 metres high. Sion is regarded as one of the sunniest towns in Switzerland, and a lot of **wine** grows on the slopes.

Above the town rise two rocky hills: **Valère** and **Tourbillon**. On Valère stands a fortified church, the **Basilica of Valère**. On Tourbillon stands a **castle ruin**. The two hills are the landmark of Sion. From the top you have a wide view over the Rhone valley.

In the Basilica of Valère stands one of the **oldest playable organs** in the world. It dates from around 1430. The organ is still played at **concerts** today. That is why music lovers come to Sion from many countries. The organ shows how long music has been made in Sion.

Near Sion the **Val d'Hérens**, in German **Eringertal**, joins the Rhone valley from the south. Its stream, the **Borgne**, flows into the Rhone at Sion. In 2018 the people of the Valais voted on a credit for the Winter Olympics “**Sion 2026**”. A majority said no. Switzerland therefore withdrew the candidacy.

gewusst: For a very long time Sion has been the seat of a bishop.
The well known Eringer cow, which takes part in cow fights, comes from the Eringertal.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Park is the only national park in Switzerland. It lies in the canton of the Grisons and has protected nature for over a hundred years. Here nature may develop entirely without human interference.
wichtigste: Switzerland has exactly one national park.
It lies in the canton of the Grisons, in the Engadine.
It was founded in 1914 and is the oldest national park in the Alps.
In the park you may not pick anything, and dogs are forbidden.
From 1991 young bearded vultures were released there.
The visitor centre is in Zernez.

abschnitte.titel: The oldest park in the Alps
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Park** lies in the east of Switzerland, in the canton of the **Grisons** in the Engadine. It was founded in 1914 and is thus the **oldest national park in the Alps** and in central Europe. Since then nature there has no longer been used: there is no farming, no hunting and no forestry. Forests, meadows and streams may develop freely. Researchers observe how nature changes without people.

In the national park nature is meant to stay undisturbed. That is why you may not **pick flowers** and must stay on the marked **paths**. **Dogs** are not allowed, because they could disturb the wild animals. Making fires and camping are also forbidden. Anyone who keeps to the rules can often watch animals from close up.

In autumn you can hear the **red deer** roaring in the national park, a loud call. Chamois, ibex and marmots also live here. The **bearded vulture** had died out in the Alps. From 1991 young bearded vultures were released in the national park. Today bearded vultures once again fly over the mountains of the Engadine.

The **visitor centre** is in the village of **Zernez**. There an exhibition shows the animals and plants of the park. The highest summit in the park is the **Piz Pisoc** at 3,174 metres. The lowest point lies at about 1,400 metres. A road over the Ofen Pass runs right through the park.

gewusst: Fallen trees simply stay where they lie in the national park and become a habitat for beetles and fungi.
The Swiss National Park is about 170 square kilometres in size.

teile.einleitung: With a regular interval timetable, trains, buses and boats run at regular intervals, every hour at the same minute. Switzerland introduced it across the whole country in 1982 and has been seen as a model ever since.
wichtigste: With the regular interval timetable, trains leave every hour at the same minute.
The SBB introduced the nationwide regular interval timetable in 1982.
Samuel Stähli is regarded as an important father of the regular interval timetable.
With the integrated regular interval timetable, connections at the nodes are coordinated with one another.
At a timetable node, several lines meet at the same time.
Post buses, buses and boats are also fitted into the interval pattern.

abschnitte.text: A regular interval timetable is easy to remember. If a train leaves at 7.14, it also leaves at 8.14 and at 9.14. With the **half hourly service**, a train comes every 30 minutes, so also at 7.44. With the **quarter hourly service**, as on many **S-Bahn** lines, there are **4 departures** per hour and direction.

In **1982** the **SBB** introduced the regular interval timetable throughout the country. Before that, trains often ran at irregular times. The railway expert **Samuel Stähli** is regarded as an important father of the new timetable. Later the service was expanded further with the **Rail 2000** project, which the people had approved in 1987.

With the **integrated regular interval timetable** it is not only about single lines. The trains meet in large stations shortly before the full or half hour and leave again shortly afterwards. Such a station is called a **timetable node**. This way you can change trains comfortably. For this to work, the journey time between two nodes has to fit well.

In Switzerland, **post buses**, **buses** and **boats** are also coordinated with the interval pattern. A bus in the village runs so that you reach the train at the station. An example: the train leaves on the hour, the bus journey takes 17 minutes and changing takes 4 minutes. Then the bus has to leave at **xx.39** at the latest.

You can calculate well with the interval pattern. If a train leaves on the hour and needs **47 minutes** to the next node, it arrives there at xx.47. Until the next full hour, passengers then wait **13 minutes**. That is why planners try to bring journey times between nodes to a little under a half or a whole hour.

gewusst: Many countries have taken the Swiss regular interval timetable as a model.
Once you know your train, you often need no timetable at all, because it runs at the same minute every hour.

teile.einleitung: Lake Biel lies at the southern foot of the Jura between Biel and La Neuveville in the canton of Bern. It is known for St Peter's Island, where the philosopher Rousseau once lived, and for the vineyards on its north shore. Through the Jura Water Correction, it was greatly changed in the 19th century.
wichtigste: Lake Biel lies mostly in the canton of Bern and is about 39 square kilometres in area.
Together with Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten it is one of the three Jura lakes.
In Lake Biel lies St Peter's Island.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau found refuge there for a few weeks in 1765.
Since the Jura Water Correction, the Aare has flowed into Lake Biel.
On the north shore lie wine villages such as Twann and Ligerz.

abschnitte.text: Lake Biel lies between the Jura in the north and the **Seeland** in the south. At the eastern end lies the bilingual city of Biel/Bienne, at the western end La Neuveville. It is about 15 kilometres long and about 74 metres deep at its deepest point. The Zihl links it with Lake Neuchâtel.

**St Peter's Island** lies in the south-west of the lake and used to be a real island. Since the water level was lowered, it has been linked to Erlach by a narrow strip of land, the Heidenweg. On it stands a former monastery, which is now a hotel. The philosopher **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** spent a few weeks here in 1765, which he described as especially happy.

In the past, the Seeland was a large swamp area that was flooded again and again. With the **Jura Water Correction** in the 19th century, the Aare was diverted through the Hagneck Canal into Lake Biel. As a result the water levels of the three Jura lakes sank by about two metres. The swamp became fertile vegetable land, the so-called vegetable garden of Switzerland.

On the steep north shore, many **vines** grow on terraces. Wine villages such as Twann, Ligerz and Schernelz have beautiful old houses. A small funicular runs from Ligerz up to Prêles on the Tessenberg. A popular vineyard trail runs along the slope from Biel to La Neuveville.

About 6,000 years ago, people were already living in villages on the shore of Lake Biel. Their houses stood on wooden piles, which is why they are called **pile dwellers**. When the lake level was lowered, many remains of these settlements came to light. Since 2011, pile dwellings around the Alps have been UNESCO World Heritage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large building project that reshaped rivers and lakes in the Seeland to prevent floods.
A flat landscape between Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten.
Houses that stood on piles on the lakeshore in the Stone Age.
A piece of land almost completely surrounded by water.

gewusst: St Peter's Island is actually no longer an island at all; you can walk there.
Since the 19th century the Aare has flowed through Lake Biel; before that it flowed past it.
Biel is the largest bilingual city in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Lake Garda is the largest lake in Italy and lies on the southern edge of the Alps. In the north it is narrow and surrounded by high mountains, in the south broad and flat. With its mild climate, olive trees and reliable wind, it is a popular holiday destination, also for many families from Switzerland.
wichtigste: Lake Garda lies in northern Italy and is the largest lake in Italy.
It has an area of about 370 square kilometres and is over 50 kilometres long.
Three Italian regions border it: Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino.
In the northern part a reliable wind blows almost every day, which is why it is popular with windsurfers.
The River Sarca flows in, and the Mincio flows out to the Po.
On the shore grow olive trees, lemons and cypresses.
Well-known places on the lake are Sirmione, Riva del Garda, Malcesine and Limone sul Garda.

abschnitte.text: Lake Garda lies in northern Italy between Milan and Venice. It is about 52 kilometres long, up to about 17 kilometres wide in the south and up to about 350 metres deep. Its surface lies at only about 65 metres above sea level. On it the regions of **Lombardy**, **Veneto** and **Trentino** meet.

Lake Garda arose in the ice ages, when a mighty **glacier** from the Adige valley carved out a deep basin. In the north the lake is therefore narrow like a fjord and framed by steep rock walls. On the east shore rises the long mountain ridge of **Monte Baldo**, which a cable car climbs from Malcesine. In the south, gentle hills of moraine debris surround the broad lake.

Very regular winds blow on Lake Garda. In the morning the **Pelèr** usually blows from the north, and in the afternoon the **Ora** comes from the south. Because you can rely on the wind almost every day, the northern part around Riva del Garda and Torbole is a paradise for windsurfers, kitesurfers and sailors. In summer the water is pleasantly warm for swimming.

The big lake stores warmth, and the mountains in the north keep cold winds away. That is why the climate is so mild that olive trees, palms, cypresses and even lemons thrive. In Limone sul Garda, people used to build terraced **lemon gardens** with tall stone pillars, which were covered over in winter. A well-known olive oil is pressed from the olives by the lake.

The Romans already loved Lake Garda. In Sirmione, on a long peninsula in the south, stand the remains of a large Roman villa called the **Grottoes of Catullus**. In the Middle Ages the Scaligeri, a ruling family from Verona, built several castles on the lake, such as the moated castle of Sirmione. Near the south shore also lies the large amusement park Gardaland.

The most important inflow is the **Sarca**, which comes from the mountains of Trentino. The outflow is the Mincio, which leaves the lake at Peschiera del Garda and later joins the Po. So the water of Lake Garda finally reaches the Adriatic. The lake is also an important drinking water store for the region.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ridge of stones and rubble pushed together by a glacier.
A south wind that blows on Lake Garda almost every afternoon.
A piece of land almost completely surrounded by water and joined to the mainland on only one side.
In Italy, a large part of the country, similar to a canton in Switzerland, only usually much larger.

gewusst: At about 370 square kilometres, Lake Garda is more than four times as large as Lake Zurich.
On Lake Garda, lemons grow outdoors further north than almost anywhere else in Europe.
The name comes from the village of Garda on the east shore; the Romans called the lake Benacus.

teile.einleitung: A sea of fog is a magnificent sight: from a mountain you see a white blanket below you that looks like a sea. On the Swiss Central Plateau it often happens, especially in autumn and winter.
wichtigste: A sea of fog is a blanket of fog or low stratus that you see from above.
On the Central Plateau it is especially common in autumn and winter.
It forms in a temperature inversion: cold air below, warmer air above.
A calm high pressure area favours a sea of fog.
The upper limit is often at about 800 to 1,200 metres.
Wind or a new weather front usually clears the fog.

abschnitte.titel: What is a sea of fog?
abschnitte.text: When there is a thick blanket of fog or **low stratus** in a valley or on the Central Plateau, it looks like a sea from a mountain. The peaks stick out of it like islands. Above the fog the sun is often shining. Down in the fog, by contrast, it is grey, damp and cool.

Normally it gets colder with height. In an **inversion** it is the other way round: cold air lies below, with warmer air above. The warm layer acts like a lid. Under it the cold, moist air stays trapped, and fog forms. On the mountains it can then even be warmer than in the valley.

In **autumn and winter** the nights are long. The ground cools strongly, and the moist air gets cold. In a calm **high pressure area** it is windless and clear, so the cooling is even stronger. The cold air collects on the **Central Plateau** between the Alps and the Jura. The weak winter sun often cannot clear the fog for days.

The upper limit of the sea of fog is often at about **800 to 1,200 metres** above sea level. That is why on foggy days many people travel up to mountains for outings such as **Pilatus**, the **Rigi** or the **Napf**. There they enjoy sun and views. Only **wind** or a new **weather front** mixes the air and drives the fog away.

With **low stratus**, the grey blanket hangs at a height of a few hundred metres. Below it you can see far, but the sky is grey. **Ground fog**, by contrast, lies right on the ground. It severely limits visibility, for example in road traffic. You see a sea of fog when you stand above the layer of fog.

gewusst: In stable high pressure, fog on the Central Plateau can sometimes stay for many days in a row.
In foggy conditions, weather services often state the height of the upper limit of the fog, so that you know how far up you need to go.

teile.einleitung: The Tabular Jura is the part of the Jura in which the rock layers lie almost flat like a tabletop. It lies in the northeast of the Swiss Jura and shapes large parts of northern Switzerland.
wichtigste: In the Tabular Jura the rock layers lie almost horizontal.
It lies in the northeast of the Swiss Jura.
Large parts of the canton of Basel-Landschaft belong to it, as does the Fricktal in Aargau.
The Randen in Schaffhausen and the Ajoie in the canton of Jura are also Tabular Jura.
Typical are broad plateaus with steeply cut valleys.
The sinking of the Upper Rhine Graben broke the layers into many blocks.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the German word **Tafel**, meaning table or slab. In the Tabular Jura the rock layers were hardly folded and therefore lie almost **horizontal**. In the southwest of the Jura it looks quite different: there folded layers form long mountain chains, the **Folded Jura**. The Tabular Jura is therefore a good example of how differently a mountain range can be built.

The Tabular Jura lies in **northern Switzerland**. A large part of the canton of **Basel-Landschaft** belongs to it, and only the south of the Baselbiet lies in the Folded Jura. In Aargau the **Fricktal** between the Jura chain and the Rhine counts as Tabular Jura. In the canton of Schaffhausen the hill country of the **Randen** belongs to it, and in the west the **Ajoie** in the canton of Jura.

The rocks of the Tabular Jura were formed a very long time ago in seas. They are mainly **limestones** from the geological periods **Triassic** and **Jurassic**. Well known layers are called **Muschelkalk**, **Hauptrogenstein** and **Malm limestone**. In such limestones you often find fossils of sea creatures, for example shells.

North of Basel lies the **Upper Rhine Graben**, a broad valley that sank over a long time. This sinking began in the early **Tertiary**. In the process, the rock plates of the Tabular Jura broke up into many single pieces along fracture lines, the **faults**. Such pieces are called **blocks**. They were not folded, however.

Typical of the Tabular Jura are broad, flat **plateaus**, on which fields and meadows often lie. Streams and rivers have cut deep into the slabs. In this way valleys with **steep walls** were formed, especially beautiful to see in the Baselbiet and in Aargau. Many villages lie down in these valleys.

gewusst: Geologically, the rock layers of the Tabular Jura continue north as far as the edge of the Black Forest.
The name “Jurassic” for a geological period comes from the Jura mountains.

teile.einleitung: After the Volga, the Danube is the second-longest river in Europe. It rises in the Black Forest in Germany and flows through ten countries to the Black Sea. On its way it passes four capital cities, including Vienna and Budapest.
wichtigste: The Danube is about 2,850 kilometres long.
It rises in the Black Forest.
It flows through 10 countries, more than any other river in the world.
Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade lie on the Danube, but Prague does not.
The Danube flows into the Black Sea in a large delta.
The Inn brings water from the Engadine into the Danube.
Even in the Iron Age the Danube was an important trade route.

abschnitte.text: The **Danube** is formed in the Black Forest in south-western Germany. At Donaueschingen the source rivers **Brigach and Breg** join. From there the Danube flows east through southern Germany. At Passau the Inn joins the Danube, shortly before it enters Austria.

The Danube flows through Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine. In this way it crosses or touches ten countries, more than any other river on Earth. It often forms the **border** between two countries. After about 2,850 kilometres it reaches the Black Sea.

Four capital cities lie on the Danube: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. In **Budapest** the river separates the districts of Buda and Pest. In Vienna there is the Danube Island, a long artificial island for protection against floods and for recreation. Prague, by contrast, does not lie on the Danube but on the Vltava.

Before its mouth the Danube splits into many arms and forms the **Danube Delta**. It lies mainly in Romania and is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Pelicans, herons and many other species of birds live there. It is one of the largest wetlands in Europe.

Even in the Iron Age the Danube was a trade route. The princely seat of **Heuneburg** on the upper Danube even shows trade with the Greeks. According to ancient sources, the Helvetii lived around 100 BC between the Rhine, the Main and the Danube before they moved to the Central Plateau. Later the Danube long formed the northern border of the Roman Empire.

The **Inn** rises in the Engadine in the Grisons and joins the Danube at Passau. In this way water from Switzerland reaches the Black Sea by way of the Danube. A part of Switzerland therefore belongs to the catchment area of the Danube. Through the Main-Danube Canal, the Danube is today also linked by ship to the Rhine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mouth area in which a river divides into many arms.
A river that, together with others, forms a larger river.
A landscape with a lot of water, such as swamps, moors and reed beds.
A waterway built by people for ships.

gewusst: At Immendingen, on some days the young Danube seeps away completely into the ground, and its water flows underground to Lake Constance and so into the Rhine.
The waltz “On the Beautiful Blue Danube” by Johann Strauss is regarded as Austria's unofficial anthem.
Today, by way of canals, the Danube links the North Sea with the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The Romandie is the French speaking part of Switzerland. It lies in the west of the country and is also called western Switzerland or the Welschland.
wichtigste: In the Romandie people speak French.
It lies in the west of Switzerland on the border with France.
The people there are called Romands, and in German also Welsche.
Geneva is the largest city, Lausanne the second largest.
Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura are entirely French speaking.
Bern, Valais and Fribourg are bilingual.

abschnitte.text: The **Romandie** is the part of Switzerland where most people speak **French**. It lies in the **west** of the country and borders France. The people there are called **Romands**, a word that comes from French. Many German speaking Swiss also call the Romandie the **“Welschland”** and its people the **“Welsche”**.

The cantons of **Geneva**, **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel** and **Jura** are entirely French speaking. Three cantons have two languages: **Bern**, **Valais** and **Fribourg**. In the Valais, people speak French in the Lower Valais and German in the Upper Valais. That is why only part of the Valais belongs to the Romandie. In the canton of Bern, too, a part in the north is French speaking.

The largest city in the Romandie is **Geneva**. Many international organisations have their seat there. The second largest city is **Lausanne**, the capital of the canton of Vaud. Other important cities are Fribourg, Neuchâtel, Sion and Biel, where German and French are spoken.

In the middle of the Romandie lies **Lake Geneva**. It is the largest lake in the Romandie. Its north shore belongs to Switzerland, its **south shore** to France. On its shores lie Geneva, Lausanne and Montreux, and on the slopes many vines grow.

The imaginary border between German speaking Switzerland and the Romandie is jokingly called the **Röstigraben** (rösti ditch). It is not a real border but an image for the fact that the two parts of the country sometimes think and vote differently. Rösti is regarded as a typical dish of German speaking Switzerland. Despite such differences, both parts of the country firmly belong together.

gewusst: The town of Biel is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland, and many street signs there are in German and French.
In the Romandie people often say “septante” and “nonante” for 70 and 90, unlike in France.

teile.einleitung: Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is not a sea but the largest lake on Earth. It lies between Europe and Asia and has slightly salty water. Five countries share its shores, and in it live the sturgeon from which the famous caviar comes.
wichtigste: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth by area.
It is about 370,000 square kilometres in area, so roughly nine times as large as Switzerland.
The most important inflow is the Volga, the longest river in Europe.
It has no outflow to the sea; the water only evaporates.
Its water is salty, but only about a third as salty as sea water.
The riparian states are Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan.
Beneath the lake bed lie large reserves of oil and natural gas.

abschnitte.text: The Caspian Sea lies between the Caucasus in the west and the steppes and deserts of Central Asia in the east. It is about 1,200 kilometres long and covers about 370,000 square kilometres, more than the whole of Germany. Its surface lies about 28 metres **below sea level**. In the south it is over 1,000 metres deep, in the north by contrast very shallow.

A sea is connected with the oceans, but the Caspian Sea is surrounded by land on all sides. Experts therefore count it among the lakes, more precisely among the **endorheic lakes** without an outflow. It got the name “sea” because of its enormous size and its salty water. Its basin is a remnant of an ancient sea that millions of years ago was also connected with the Black Sea.

abschnitte.titel: The Volga and the water balance
abschnitte.text: The **Volga** supplies about four fifths of the water that flows into the lake. Other inflows are the Ural, the Terek and the Kura. Because there is no outflow, water is lost only through **evaporation**, and the salt stays behind. That is why the water is salty, but almost fresh in the north near the mouth of the Volga. The water level varies strongly over the years and has fallen recently.

In the Caspian Sea live several species of **sturgeon**, ancient-looking fish with bony plates instead of scales. Caviar, a very expensive delicacy, is made from their eggs. Because of overfishing and poaching, sturgeon are seriously endangered today. The **Caspian seal** also lives here, the only seal species far away from any ocean.

On the shore lie large cities such as Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, and Astrakhan in Russia. Near Baku, **oil** has been extracted for over 150 years, and today there are drilling platforms in the middle of the lake. For a long time the five riparian states argued over who owns which part of the lake. In 2018 they signed a treaty that settles many of these questions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lake without an outflow, whose water disappears only through evaporation.
A country that borders a lake, a sea or a river.
A very old, large fish with bony plates, whose eggs are used to make caviar.
When water turns through warmth into invisible water vapour and rises into the air.

gewusst: The Caspian Sea is larger than the five Great Lakes of North America put together.
The bay of Kara-Bogaz-Gol on the east shore is so salty that hardly any living thing can survive there.
The beluga, a sturgeon from the Caspian Sea, is among the largest freshwater fish in the world and can grow several metres long.

teile.einleitung: The Doubs is a river in the Jura mountains that flows through France and Switzerland. Over a long stretch it forms the border between the two countries. It makes such a big loop that its source and its mouth lie surprisingly close together.
wichtigste: The Doubs is about 450 kilometres long.
It rises in the French Jura.
On one section it forms the border between Switzerland and France.
At Les Brenets it plunges about 27 metres in the Saut du Doubs.
In the canton of Jura it flows past the old town of Saint-Ursanne.
The Doubs flows into the Saône.

abschnitte.text: The **Doubs** rises near Mouthe in the French Jura. It first flows north-east and then, between Les Brenets and the canton of Jura, forms the **border** between Switzerland and France. At Saint-Ursanne it flows for a stretch through Switzerland and then returns to France in a sharp bend. By way of the city of Besançon it turns south-west and joins the **Saône**.

At Les Brenets the river widens into the narrow **Lac des Brenets**. At the end of the lake the water plunges about 27 metres in the **Saut du Doubs**. The waterfall is a popular destination that can be reached by boat. In very cold winters the lake sometimes freezes over.

In the canton of Jura, the medieval little town of **Saint-Ursanne** lies on the Doubs. It has an old stone bridge, town gates and a beautiful collegiate church. The loop that the river makes there is called the Clos du Doubs. Above the valley lie the Franches-Montagnes with their pastures and horses.

The valley of the Doubs is deeply cut and densely wooded. In the river lives the rare **Roi du Doubs**, a fish found nowhere else in the world. It is threatened with extinction. Power plants and pollution are causing problems for the river, so Switzerland and France work together on its protection.

The Saône flows into the **Rhône** in Lyon. So the water of the Doubs finally reaches the Mediterranean. A French département bears the name Doubs. The border region is French-speaking, on both sides of the river.

begriffe.erklaerung: A river that forms the border between two countries.
A place where a river plunges down over a rock step.
A big bend that a river makes in the landscape.
An administrative district in France, similar to a canton.

gewusst: Although the Doubs is about 450 kilometres long, its source and mouth are only about 90 kilometres apart as the crow flies.
The fish Roi du Doubs means “King of the Doubs” in translation.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Federal Railways, SBB for short, are the largest railway company in Switzerland. Their red trains run through the whole country. The SBB belong to the Confederation and carry very many people and goods every day.
wichtigste: The SBB began operating in 1902.
In French they are called CFF, in Italian FFS.
SBB trains run on electricity, a large part of it from hydropower.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long and opened in 2016.
The station clock by Hans Hilfiker has a red second hand.
With the General Abonnement (GA) you can travel almost everywhere for a year.

abschnitte.titel: A railway for the whole of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In the past the railways in Switzerland belonged to various private companies. In 1902 the **SBB** began operating as the railway of the Confederation. In French they are called “Chemins de fer fédéraux”, **CFF** for short, and in Italian **FFS**. Many SBB locomotives and trains are **red**, and their logo is red too. The SBB have their headquarters in Bern.

SBB trains run on **electricity**. A large part of their power is generated by the SBB themselves with **hydropower**, for example with reservoirs in the mountains. The standard gauge network has a **track gauge** of 1,435 millimetres between the rails. This gauge is the same in most countries of Europe, so trains can also travel abroad. The largest station in Switzerland is **Zurich Main Station**.

Switzerland has many railway tunnels because the Alps are in the way. The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is about 57 kilometres long and opened in 2016. It is (as of 2026) the longest railway tunnel in the world. Because it lies deep down in the mountain, the trains hardly have to climb. This way you get from north to south more quickly.

The engineer **Hans Hilfiker** designed the SBB station clock in the 1940s. Later he added the typical **red second hand** with the round dot. At the 12 this hand stops briefly before all the clocks carry on together. In this way the clocks in all stations show exactly the same time. The clock is regarded today as a classic of Swiss design.

With the **General Abonnement**, **GA** for short, you can use almost all trains, buses and trams in Switzerland for a whole year. Many people also have a **Half Fare Card**, with which they get tickets more cheaply. The **regular interval timetable** ensures that many trains run every hour at the same minute. This makes it easy to change trains, and you have little to remember about the times.

gewusst: On the SBB station clock the second hand waits briefly at the 12 until the minute hand jumps one step on.
The SBB run their own hydroelectric power stations to generate railway power.

teile.einleitung: Lake Sils lies high up in the Upper Engadine in the canton of the Grisons. It is the largest of the Upper Engadine lakes. Its landscape has inspired many artists and thinkers.
wichtigste: Lake Sils lies in the Upper Engadine between Maloja and Sils.
It lies just under 1,800 metres above sea level.
In Romansh it is called Lej da Segl.
The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche spent several summers in Sils Maria.
A scheduled boat has run on the lake since 1907.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Sils** lies in the **Upper Engadine** between **Maloja** and **Sils**. It is the largest of the Upper Engadine lakes. Because it lies just under **1,800 metres above sea level**, it mostly freezes over in winter. In the Engadine people speak **Romansh**. Sils is called Segl there, and “Lej” means lake, which is why it is called **Lej da Segl**.

Since 1907 a **scheduled boat** has run on Lake Sils between Sils and Maloja. It passes the **Chastè peninsula**, which juts far into the lake. In autumn the mysterious **Sils balls** are sometimes washed up on the shore. They are made of **larch needles** and grow up to 30 centimetres in size. Exactly how they form has not yet been fully researched.

The philosopher **Friedrich Nietzsche** came to **Sils Maria** several times from 1881. He valued the peace and the clear air and wrote his works there. His house is now a **museum**, the Nietzsche House. Painters and writers, too, have drawn inspiration from the landscape by the lake.

gewusst: The Sils balls of larch needles are almost round like balls.
In winter you can sometimes go cross country skiing on the frozen lake.
